Some predict the disappearance of millions of jobs; others promise a new positive revolution.
The truth likely lies somewhere in between.
Machines are now capable of performing tasks that were once thought to be reserved for humans: writing texts, analyzing images, answering questions.
However, it would be an exaggeration to think that they will replace everything.
Artificial intelligence succeeds where a lot of information needs to be processed quickly.
It still fails when it comes to understanding a human situation, showing creativity, or making a difficult decision.
The most likely scenario is that many jobs will change rather than disappear.
We will need to learn to work with these tools, just as we once learned to use the computer.
The real question may not be whether the machine will replace us, but what we will choose to entrust to it.

sentences: In October, in front of my house, the swallows gather on the power lines.
There are dozens of them, then hundreds.
And then, one morning, they are no longer there.
Gone.
Where do they go?
Very far: to Africa, across the sea.
Every autumn, millions of birds leave Europe and fly south.
This great journey is called migration.
Why do they leave?
Because of food.
Swallows eat insects, and in winter, here, the insects disappear.
So the birds go where it's warm.
The journey is incredible and dangerous.
Some birds fly thousands of kilometers, over the sea and mountains.
Many travel in groups: it's safer, and the young learn the route with the adults.
But the most amazing thing is the return.
In spring, the swallows come back, and often they find exactly the same nest as the year before!
Without a map, without a phone.
Scientists think they use the sun, the stars, and the Earth's magnetic field.
So in spring, when the first swallows arrive in your sky, think of their journey.
These little birds weighing twenty grams come back from Africa, and they may have been born under your roof.

sentences: Few subjects spark as intense debates as the electric car.
For some, it is the savior of the planet, the end of pollution, a finally clean future.
For others, it is a vast illusion, an ecological lie disguised as progress.
As is often the case when positions harden, the truth lies in a less comfortable but fairer middle ground: the electric car is a real but partial advancement — neither a miracle nor a sham.
Let's start with its advantages, which are undeniable.
An electric car emits no exhaust gases where it drives.

In cities, where air pollution causes respiratory diseases and premature deaths, this point is far from trivial: replacing gasoline engines with electric ones would significantly improve the health of millions of city dwellers.
Moreover, it is silent, which alleviates another often overlooked urban pollution: noise.
On these two fronts, the gain is clear and immediate.
But the picture becomes more nuanced as soon as we broaden our view beyond the tailpipe.
A car is not just what it emits while driving; it is also what was needed to manufacture it.
However, the production of an electric car, particularly its battery, is very energy-intensive and requires rare metals, the extraction of which poses serious environmental and human issues.
Upon leaving the factory, an electric car already has a heavier 'carbon footprint' than a conventional one.
It only starts to be advantageous after tens of thousands of kilometers, once this debt is repaid by the absence of emissions during use.
A second, decisive caveat: an electric car is only as good as the electricity that powers it.
Charged with clean energy, it lives up to its promise.
Charged with coal-fired power, it merely shifts pollution from the street to the chimney.
Its balance sheet therefore entirely depends on how each country produces its electricity — which leads to very different assessments from one region of the world to another.
Thus, the electric car is a conditional advancement: it will be truly beneficial if electricity becomes decarbonized and if batteries become cheaper to produce and easier to recycle.
These conditions are partly being met, which invites a measured optimism rather than blind enthusiasm or outright rejection.
There remains a more troubling question that the enthusiasm for the electric car conveniently allows us to avoid.
What if the real problem isn't the type of engine, but the number of cars?
Replacing hundreds of millions of gasoline cars one by one with electric ones perpetuates a model based on individual car ownership, with its traffic jams, confiscated space, and drained resources.
Developing public transport, cycling, and cities where one can live without a car: these are often more effective solutions, but less appealing, as they cannot be sold at dealerships.
The electric car therefore deserves its place — provided we do not mistake it for what it is not: the end of the problem.
At best, it is part of the solution.

sentences: On Monday, the region presented a plan aimed at reducing household waste by 15% over five years.
The program is based on three main areas: developing composting, encouraging the repair of items, and helping municipalities better inform residents.
On paper, the plan seems to have broad support.
No one seriously defends the idea of producing even more waste.
However, its implementation is likely to be less straightforward than a simple awareness poster.
Installing communal composters requires space, maintenance, and residents willing to change their habits.
Repair workshops, on the other hand, require facilities, trained volunteers, and real visibility.
Environmental organizations therefore welcome the overall direction while calling for clearer resources.
They fear that the wealthier municipalities will progress quickly, while others will remain with good intentions.
Several rural mayors also raise the issue of transportation: in a village, getting to a repair workshop may require a car.
The region promises an initial assessment in a year.
This will be the time to see if the plan truly changes practices or if it remains a reasonable ambition, but too general.

sentences: To stay healthy, you need to move.
But be careful: that doesn't mean running a marathon or spending hours in a gym.
Moving a little every day is already enough to do a lot of good for the body.
The problem with modern life is that we sit all day: sitting at work, sitting in the car, sitting in front of the television.
However, the human body is not made for immobility.
Without exercise, the muscles weaken and energy decreases.
The good news is that a little regular effort is better than a big effort now and then.
Walking for twenty minutes a day, taking the stairs instead of the elevator, getting off the bus one stop earlier: these small habits make a real difference.
The heart works, the muscles wake up, and you feel fitter.
Moving is not only good for the body; it's also good for your mood.
After a walk, even a short one, you often feel calmer and in a better mood.
Mental fatigue from the day decreases.
The secret is to choose an activity you enjoy: walking, dancing, cycling, gardening.
When an activity is a pleasure, you repeat it effortlessly.
And it's regularity, more than intensity, that keeps the body healthy for life.

sentences: On Thursday evenings at seven o'clock, one sacred thing awaits me: basketball.
We play in an old gymnasium, behind the town hall.
The floor creaks and the heating works every other day.
The team is an unlikely mix.
There is Paul, two meters tall, who has never played sports before he turned forty.
There is Sonia, small and as fast as lightning, the best of us.
And there is me, neither tall nor fast, but motivated.
Last night, an important match: the 'Foxes' against the 'Eagles'.
We made up the names, but on the court, everyone plays like it's the finals.
The first half was tough.
The Eagles were leading by ten points.
Sonia gathered us together: 'We defend better, we pass faster, and we believe in it!'
The second half was crazy.
Paul blocked three shots.
Sonia was stealing balls everywhere.
And I scored two baskets!
My record of the season.
We lost by three points.
My winning shot spun on the rim and came out.
The Eagles shouted with joy.
And then, like every Thursday, winners and losers went to the café across the street.
An hour of laughter and 'next week, we will destroy you'.
We play basketball, officially.
In truth, we maintain a friendship.
On Thursday evenings, that matters more than the score.

sentences: Each inhabitant of a wealthy country throws away, on average, nearly half a ton of waste per year.
Put together, this waste forms an invisible mountain that we prefer not to look at: once the trash is taken out, the problem seems to disappear.
But it doesn't disappear; it just moves.
Where does our waste go?
Some of it is burned, which in turn produces emissions.
Another part ends up in enormous landfills, where certain materials, like plastic, will take centuries to decompose.
Finally, a portion is recycled — but much less than we think.
Sorting our waste is a useful gesture, and we must continue to do it; but recycling has its limits.
It costs energy, and many items simply cannot be recycled.
That's why specialists remind us of an uncomfortable truth: the best waste is the one we don't produce.
Before recycling, we should primarily reduce.
However, our way of life is going in the opposite direction.
We consume more and more items, often packaged multiple times, often designed to be thrown away quickly.
Waste is not an accident of the system; it is part of it.
What can we do, concretely?
On an individual scale, a few habits significantly reduce our waste: refusing unnecessary packaging, buying in bulk, repairing instead of replacing, avoiding single-use items.
These actions alone will not save the planet — we shouldn't fool ourselves.
But they change our perspective, and they send a signal.
For the real lever is broader.
It is the companies that decide on packaging, and the governments that set the rules.
A citizen who reduces their waste is also a consumer and a voter who pushes, in their own way, in the right direction.
The mountain of our waste is not a fatality: it is the result of billions of small decisions, and these decisions can change.

It's the best place in the room.
I see the neighbor's garden.

I love this moment.
On the walls, there are posters.
There is also a small green plant.
Its name is Georges.
Yes, I gave my plant a name.
In the evening, I close the door, turn on my lamp, and read.
Here, I am peaceful.
It's my little world.
For a long time, I never cooked fish.
I was scared: I didn't know how to choose it or how to prepare it.
I always bought meat.
One Saturday, at the market, I stopped in front of the fishmonger.
There were a lot of fish on the ice.
I looked at them without understanding.
The fishmonger saw me.
"Can I help you?"
I was honest: "I would like to try, but I don't know anything about fish."
He smiled.
"Then I will explain to you."
He showed me how to choose fresh fish.
"Look at the eyes: they should be clear, not gray.
And smell: fresh fish hardly smells at all."
Then, he recommended a simple fish to start with.
"Take this one.
You put it in the oven for twenty minutes with lemon, oil, and a little salt.
Don't do anything complicated."
He prepared it for me and wrapped it up.

sentences: Two years ago, we decided to adopt a dog.

He moved from the door to the living room rug, then to the couch.

It's the only direct route between the north and south of the city.

sentences: Before each trip, I learn about twenty words in the language of the country.
Not complicated phrases: hello, thank you, please, excuse me, yes, no, how much, where is, I don't understand, goodbye.
It takes about two hours in total.
And the effect is disproportionate.
The first time I noticed this was in Greece.
I had learned 'hello' and 'thank you' on the plane.
In a small grocery store, I used them awkwardly, with a certainly terrible accent.
The shopkeeper, who spoke English, immediately changed his attitude.
He smiled, corrected my pronunciation while laughing, and offered me a fruit.
Why such a difference for two words?
I believe the reason is simple.
These words don't really serve to communicate: English would have been enough.
They serve to say something else: 'I know I am in your country, and I am making an effort.'
It's a form of politeness, and politeness has always been more of a signal than information.
The opposite is also true.
A traveler who arrives and immediately speaks English, assuming that everyone understands him, sends a message too — even if he doesn't realize it.
I don't speak any of the languages of the countries I have visited correctly.
I don't claim otherwise.
But I have never regretted those two hours.
And even years later, I still sometimes remember the word 'thank you' in Hungarian.

sentences: Few words come up as often in the French public debate as the word laïcité.
Few are as regularly misunderstood, both in France and abroad.
The principle takes its current form from the law of 1905, which separates the Churches and the State.
This law put an end to a system where the State financed and regulated certain religions.
It is based on two ideas, often cited separately even though they go together.
The first is the neutrality of the State.
The public authority does not recognize, pay, or subsidize any religion.
A civil servant, in the exercise of their duties, does not express their religious beliefs.
The second is the freedom of conscience.
The State guarantees the free exercise of religions.
In other words, laïcité was not designed against religions, but to allow their coexistence without any one occupying the State.
The most common misunderstanding is to confuse these two levels.
Neutrality applies to the State and its agents, not to individuals in the public space.
A user of a public service is not subject to the same obligations as an agent.

There are also some little-known historical exceptions: in Alsace and Moselle, which were attached to Germany in 1905, a previous concordat regime still applies, and some religions are financed there.
Contemporary debates rarely focus on the principle itself, which is widely accepted.
They focus on its concrete application — in schools, in sports, at work.
That is to say, as often, not on the rule, but on its boundaries.

sentences: A cultural difference often strikes the British living in France: their attitude towards time off.
In France, taking all of one's vacation is taken for granted.
No one makes excuses for it, and an employee who didn't take their days off would actually worry those around them.
In the UK as well as in the United States, it's not uncommon for employees to leave days unused.
Some companies even implicitly praised this, as commitment was measured by availability.
This difference is very concretely evident in August.
Part of the country slows down: artisans close for three weeks, files wait for the return, and it becomes difficult to get an administrative decision.
For a newcomer, this is confusing, even frustrating.
Tom spent an August getting annoyed that no one was responding to his emails.
His colleague replied to him upon his return: 'I was on vacation.'
This response, in France, is complete.
It requires neither excuse nor justification.
Behind this lies an idea that structures a large part of French work culture: time outside of work is not a leftover, it's a legitimate part of life.
The right to disconnect, established by law since 2017, extends this logic.
It would be naive to idealize this model: France also experiences burnout, and some sectors practice it intensely.
But the social norm, on the other hand, is different.
After six years in France, Tom now takes all his vacation.
'At first, I felt guilty,' he says.
'Now, I find it normal.'

sentences: A large majority of people look for medical information online before, or sometimes instead of, consulting a doctor.
This practice is often mocked.
It deserves a more nuanced view.
It has real advantages.
An informed patient asks better questions, understands better what is explained to them, and is more willing to follow a treatment whose logic they grasp.
For chronic illnesses, online patient communities provide concrete help that the healthcare system does not always offer.
But it has two well-identified pitfalls.
The first is statistical.
Search engines do not rank results by medical probability.
A headache can correspond to dozens of causes, most of which are benign; however, it is the serious causes that appear, because they generate more content.
The result is disproportionate anxiety, sometimes called 'cyberchondria.'
The second is the unequal quality of sources.
Commercial sites, unmoderated forums, and promotional content sit alongside serious resources, without the presentation always allowing them to be distinguished.
A few reflexes can limit these risks.
Favor institutional sites or public health organizations.
Be wary of any content that simultaneously sells a solution.
Check the date: medical recommendations evolve.
And above all, keep in mind a fundamental limit.
A search engine lists possibilities.
A doctor examines a person, knows their history, and rules out the vast majority of these possibilities in a few minutes.
It is not the same operation.

sentences: The sky is blue during the day and often red or orange at sunset.
These two phenomena, which seem separate, actually come from the same cause.
Sunlight appears white, but it is made up of all colors.
Each color corresponds to a different wavelength: blue and violet are short, while red is long.
When this light passes through the atmosphere, it encounters countless air molecules.
These molecules scatter the light, and this scattering phenomenon does not affect all colors in the same way: short colors, like blue, are scattered much more than long colors.
As a result, in the middle of the day: blue is sent in all directions of the sky, so when you look up, you see it everywhere.
Violet is even more scattered, but our eyes are less sensitive to it and some of it is absorbed in the upper atmosphere.
In the evening, the situation changes.
The sun is low, and its light passes through a much thicker layer of atmosphere.
On this long journey, blue is scattered so early that it no longer reaches our eyes directly.
Only the long colors remain, red and orange, which is why sunsets are that color.
This also explains a common observation: sunsets are particularly red when the air contains more particles — dust, pollution, ash.
This mechanism, described in the nineteenth century, illustrates an interesting idea.
A color is not just a property of light.
It is the result of a journey, and what it encountered along the way.

sentences: For the first time in history, a large part of humanity can listen to music almost without interruption.
In transport, at work, while walking, while cooking, with headphones on.
This omnipresence is recent.
For centuries, music was rare: it was heard at a party, in church, when someone played.
Listening to it was an event.
What does this continuous listening do to us?
Its positive effects are well documented.
Music affects mood, often effectively: an upbeat song can really change a mindset.
It facilitates physical effort, which athletes know well.
It helps with concentration for certain tasks, especially in a noisy environment that it helps to mask.
It also has a close link with memory.
A song can bring back, intact, a memory that is twenty years old.
This property is used in medicine: for people who have lost a large part of their memories, music from their youth sometimes revives their gaze and words.
But constant listening may have a cost that is less studied.
By filling every moment, it eliminates silence — those empty moments where the mind wanders, where ideas come.
It also transforms music into background noise: by listening all the time, we no longer really listen.
Some musicians regret this: their art, designed to be the center of attention, has become a backdrop.
There is no moral conclusion to draw from this.
Perhaps only an invitation.
To listen, sometimes, to a single piece, without doing anything else.

sentences: "Buying local" has become a common piece of advice, almost a reflex.
The idea seems obvious: a product that comes from nearby has traveled less, and therefore has polluted less.
The reality is more nuanced.
The benefits of local products are real.
It supports local producers, often guarantees fresher products, and maintains local agriculture.
These reasons are enough to defend it.
But from a strictly climate perspective, the situation is more complicated.
Transport actually represents only a small part of the footprint of most foods — often less than ten percent.
The key lies in the way of producing.
A telling example: a tomato grown next door, but in a heated greenhouse in the middle of winter, can have a much larger footprint than a tomato from a sunny country transported by ship.
The heating of the greenhouse weighs more than the journey.
Similarly, the mode of transport is very important.
The ship carries large quantities with low emissions per kilo; the airplane, on the other hand, is disastrous.
A distant product that arrives by cargo can be more sustainable than a regional product transported by plane.
What matters most, ultimately, is the season.
The fairest formula can be summed up in two words: local and in season.
The May strawberry from your region, yes; the December strawberry, no, whether it comes from far away or from a nearby greenhouse.
So it’s not about giving up on local products, which have many virtues.
It’s about not believing that a single word on a label solves the issue.
Geographical common sense must be accompanied by a calendar.

sentences: People often learn a language for a practical reason: work, a trip, an exam.
These are good reasons.
But those who go further generally discover something else, something harder to name.
A language is not just a code for saying the same things differently.
Each language slices the world in its own way.
Some distinguish colors that others group together.
Some have a specific word for an emotion that elsewhere requires a whole sentence.
French distinguishes between 'tu' and 'vous', a distinction that doesn't exist in English and subtly changes every relationship.
Learning a language is therefore discovering categories that you didn't have before.
There is also a troubling experience reported by many bilingual people: they don't feel quite the same depending on the language they speak.
More direct in one, more reserved in the other.
As if each language activates a slightly different version of oneself.
It's not magic.
A language is tied to a culture, to situations, to memories.
Speaking it means entering a little into that world.
Finally, there is the simple, concrete pleasure of crossing a threshold.
The day you understand a joke, follow a fast conversation, or dream in the other language.
That moment rewards months of thankless effort.
These benefits are not promised at the beginning.
You can't sell them, because they only reveal themselves along the way.
Maybe that's why they matter.
A language doesn't just add a tool to your toolbox.
It adds a window to your house.

sentences: Never before has humanity had access to so much information.
At any hour, from anywhere, we can know what is happening on the other side of the world, almost in real time.
This abundance should make us exceptionally well-informed citizens.
However, nothing is less certain, and it may even be that the opposite is true.
The first problem lies in the volume.
A continuous stream of information does not allow time to digest it.
Barely have we grasped one event before another pushes it aside, then another still.
This succession creates the illusion of following the world, while it prevents us from understanding it.
Understanding requires perspective, connections, and context — everything that speed forbids.
The second problem lies in the nature of what captures our attention.
In a saturated space, only the most striking content floats to the surface: the dramatic, the scandalous, the shocking.
Not because they are the most important, but because they catch the eye.
Thus, a distorted image of the world forms, where the exceptional seems ordinary and where slow, yet decisive, changes remain invisible due to their lack of spectacle.
A third problem, more insidious, concerns our emotions.
Continuous information keeps us in a state of permanent alertness, mixing anxiety, anger, and helplessness.
However, a constantly agitated mind judges poorly.
Overwhelmed by anxiety-inducing news over which we have no control, we often end up feeling overwhelmed without any action resulting from it.
Should we then cut ourselves off from current events?
That would be a reverse error, as staying informed remains a duty in a democracy.
The solution is not to know less, but to know differently.
It is better to read a few in-depth analyses than to swallow dozens of brief articles; it is better to choose our moments of information than to endure a constant flow.
Truly staying informed requires an effort that the ease of continuous flow makes us forget.
Being exposed to information is not the same as understanding it, and confusing the two means believing oneself to be enlightened while merely flailing in the dark.

sentences: A recipe is never just a list of ingredients and actions.
It carries within it a story, that of a region, a family, a time.

The dish that a grandmother passes on to her grandchildren is not just food: it is a fragment of memory, a connection to those who cooked it before, a way to preserve a bit of what, without it, would disappear.
In this sense, cooking is a heritage, but a particular heritage: alive, fragile, that only exists as long as it is practiced.
This is what distinguishes it from a monument or a painting.
A cathedral remains even if no one looks at it; a recipe, on the other hand, dies as soon as we stop making it.
It is not preserved in a museum, but in hands that repeat actions, in a transmission that plays out from one generation to the next.
Break this chain, and a whole body of knowledge vanishes, often without us realizing it until it’s too late.
However, this transmission is now under threat.
Time is lacking, lifestyles have changed, and it has become so easy to buy ready-made that we cook less and less.
What’s the point of learning a dish that takes a long time to prepare when you can, in just a few minutes, get an equivalent?
The question seems reasonable, but it overlooks what is lost in the exchange: not just a flavor, but a know-how and the connection it carried.
It is not about condemning convenience, nor about insisting that everyone spend hours at the stove.
Modern life has its constraints, and one can legitimately rely, sometimes, on ease.
But it would be a shame to let this domestic art completely disappear, on the pretext that it is no longer necessary.
For what is no longer necessary is not therefore without value.
Cooking for oneself, passing on a recipe, learning a dish from one's family: these modest actions maintain a precious link with the past and with others.
They remind us that eating is not just a function, but a culture.
Preserving this living heritage requires neither law nor museum: only that, from time to time, someone takes the time to do and to show.

sentences: A difficult question runs through our relationship with the past: can we judge those who came before us by our own values?
When we discover that admired figures committed or tolerated what seems unacceptable to us today, how should we react?
Should we condemn them in the name of our principles, or excuse them on the grounds that they were of their time?
The question does not have a simple answer, and the two extreme positions turn out, upon examination, to be equally unsatisfactory.
The first position is to judge the past without leniency, to apply our current values to those who lived in the past, and to condemn without appeal what offends us.
This attitude has a moral requirement: it refuses to turn a blind eye to real injustices on the pretext that they are old.
But it has a major flaw: it is anachronistic.
It blames people of the past for not sharing ideas that did not yet exist, for not seeing what no one, or almost no one, could see at the time.
It judges without understanding, from a position of easy superiority.
The second, opposite position is to excuse everything in the name of context: 'they were of their time,' it is said, as if that were enough to absolve them.
This attitude has a sense of historical nuance: it reminds us that people of the past thought within a framework that was not ours.

But when taken to extremes, it becomes a comfortable relativism that forbids any judgment, and ultimately admits that nothing, ever, could be condemned, since everything could be explained by its time.
If everything is excusable, then the worst is too.
Between these two dead ends, a fairer path is to distinguish between understanding and approving.
We can understand why people of the past thought and acted as they did, place their actions in context, and measure what they could or could not conceive — without approving what remains condemnable.
Understanding is not excusing; it is refusing lazy judgment while retaining the ability to judge.
We can recognize that an injustice was an injustice, while taking into account the blindness of the time.
This distinction also allows for a form of humility.
For if we judge harshly the blindness of our ancestors, we should remember that we too have our blind spots, which future generations may judge with the same severity.
Today, we likely tolerate things that will one day seem scandalous.
Judging the past should therefore make us not arrogant, but clear-sighted about our own time.
Judging the past with today's eyes is thus both necessary and perilous.
Necessary, because to renounce all judgment would be to renounce morality; perilous, because judging without understanding is unjust.
Wisdom consists in holding both: understanding without absolving, judging without believing oneself superior.
And never to forget that we will, in turn, be judged.

sentences: We are naturally impressed by those who speak well.
Eloquence, mastery of words, and fluency of speech command our respect and lead us to attribute intelligence and insight to those who possess them.
This association between speaking well and thinking well is deeply ingrained in us.
But it deserves to be questioned, because the link between the quality of expression and that of thought is more uncertain than we believe, and can even, at times, be reversed.
There is, of course, a grain of truth in this association.
Clearly expressing an idea often implies having conceived it clearly; the confusion of the message frequently betrays the confusion of thought.
Knowing how to order one's words, distinguish, nuance, and argue are operations that pertain to both thought and language.
In this sense, speaking well can be a sign that one thinks well, and the effort to express oneself better is often an effort to think better.
Language and thought are linked, and working on one helps the other.
But this association has its limits, and even its pitfalls.
For eloquence is also an art that can be cultivated independently of the correctness of ideas.
One can learn to speak beautifully without saying anything, to dress hollow or false thoughts in beautiful words.
History is full of brilliant orators serving despicable causes, in superb speeches that have led to the worst misguidances.
Eloquence is a power, and like any power, it is morally neutral: it serves both truth and falsehood with the same effectiveness.
There is something even more disturbing.
Eloquence can not only mask the absence of thought but actively deceive judgment.
A skillful speech moves, seduces, and carries away, and this seduction weakens the critical mind of the listener.
We are inclined to believe what is well said, to confuse the beauty of form with the truth of content.
Manipulators know this well, as they carefully craft their rhetoric precisely to disarm our vigilance.
The charm of words can be the best ally of lies.
Conversely, a correct thought can be expressed clumsily.
Many people who think deeply express themselves without brilliance, hesitate, search for their words, and we wrongly judge them as mediocre because they lack fluency.
Thus, we risk preferring a hollow smooth talker to a clumsy but correct thinker, deceived by form at the expense of content.
The seduction of eloquence can make us unjust towards the poorly dressed truth.
Speaking well is therefore neither a guarantee nor proof of thinking well.
Sometimes it is a sign, sometimes a mask.
Wisdom consists in not being dazzled by form, in seeking the solidity of ideas beneath the words, and in being wary of our own tendency to believe what is well said.
Not to despise eloquence — which, in the service of truth, is precious — but to never confuse it with the truth that it can serve as well as betray.

sentences: Our relationship with animals is full of contradictions that we rarely notice.
We cherish certain animals like family members, we are outraged by the suffering of some species, while we raise and eat others without thinking about it.
We mourn a dog and cut up a pig, without always realizing how strange this difference in treatment can be.
Questioning this inconsistency is not being sentimental; it is asking what we really owe to the sentient beings that share the world with us.
The starting point is a fact that science has firmly established: many animals are sentient beings, capable of feeling pain, fear, and undoubtedly forms of well-being.
It is no longer a sentimental hypothesis, but a fact.
Now, if a being can suffer, its suffering counts morally — this is a principle that is hard to refute.
We all admit that it is wrong to make an animal suffer unnecessarily; we therefore recognize, at least implicitly, that their suffering has value, that it obliges us to something.
But how far does this obligation go?
This is where the difficulties begin, and where our intuitions become muddled.
Should we treat all sentient animals equally, from dogs to pigs, from cats to chickens?
Logic would suggest so, but our habits refuse it.
We establish hierarchies between species that often owe more to custom, affection, or utility than to real differences in sensitivity.
The pig is no less sensitive than the dog; if we treat them so differently, it is not on the basis of a clear principle, but out of cultural habit.
Recognizing this inconsistency does not necessarily lead to a single conclusion.
Some conclude that we must stop making animals suffer and killing them for our use; others believe that we can continue to use them, but by reducing their suffering and respecting certain limits.
Between these positions, the debate is open and legitimate.
But what seems difficult to defend is the thoughtless status quo: treating sentient beings in radically opposite ways without ever questioning what justifies it.
What is certain is that the extent of the animal suffering we inflict can no longer be ignored.

The conditions in which most animals intended for our consumption are raised and slaughtered clash, when faced directly, with the very principle we recognize: that it is wrong to cause unnecessary suffering.
Whether we choose to give up this consumption or to transform it deeply, it becomes difficult to continue it while turning a blind eye.
Loving animals, how far?
The question does not call for a simple answer, but it does call for a coherent, or at least thoughtful, response.
We can no longer be satisfied with loving some and ignoring the fate of others, as if our spontaneous feelings could serve as morality.
Taking animal sensitivity seriously means accepting to question our habits and to align our actions a bit more with what, deep down, we already know.

sentences: When night falls and most residents head home, one thinks the city is asleep.
It is not.
Another city awakens then, different from the one during the day, populated by beings and activities that are not usually seen.
The urban night has its own life, its inhabitants, its rhythms, and exploring it means discovering a hidden side of the city, often ignored by those who only know its daytime face.
The nocturnal city is primarily one of invisible work.
While the majority sleeps, a crowd of men and women ensures the city runs: hospital caregivers, street and office cleaners, factory workers who never stop, drivers, bakers, guards.
This essential nighttime work is done in the shadows, unnoticed by those who, in the morning, will find the city clean, the transport ready, the bread warm, without wondering who made it possible.
The night reveals a whole laboring population that the day conceals.
The nocturnal city is also one of celebration and pleasure.
When work ends, others seek in the night what the day does not offer them: freedom, connection, forgetfulness, intoxication.
The nightlife spots come alive, a youth gathers there, a particular sociability unfolds, freer, sometimes more intense than that of the day.
The night has always been the time of permitted transgression, where the rules loosen, where one can be a little different from who they are during the day.
But the urban night also has its shadow.

It is the time of solitude for those who traverse it without sleep; the time of fear for those who dare not go out; the time when the most disadvantaged, the homeless, take refuge, for whom the nocturnal city is not a choice but a deprivation.
The night that liberates some exposes others, and the same darkness can be a celebration or distress depending on whether one traverses it for pleasure or necessity.
This dual nature of the urban night makes it a revealer.

What happens in the city after nightfall says a lot about what this city is: how it treats those who work at night, how it welcomes or pushes away those who inhabit it, how it lights up or abandons its dark streets.
The night paradoxically highlights what the day hides: inequalities, solitude, but also freedoms and solidarities of a city.
Looking at the city at night is therefore seeing it differently, in a truth that the day covers.
It is discovering that a city is never entirely what one believes, that it leads, in the shadows, a parallel existence, made of labor and celebration, of freedom and distress.
The city never sleeps; it only changes its face, and this nocturnal face deserves to be learned to be seen.

sentences: A quiet upheaval is transforming our societies: they are aging.
We are living longer and having fewer children; this double movement results in a population with an increasing average age, where older people are becoming more numerous compared to the young.
This phenomenon, often presented as a threat, deserves a more nuanced examination, as it is both a real challenge and, in many ways, a sign of success.
Let's start with the positive aspects, which are too often overlooked in alarmist discourse.
If we are aging, it is primarily because we are living longer — which is a wonderful achievement.
The fact that life expectancy has increased so much, that old age has become a long stage of existence rather than a rarity, reflects the progress in medicine, hygiene, and living standards.
We cannot simply lament an aging population that partly results from the fortunate fact that death is receding.
The first face of aging is one of victory over early death.
That said, this aging presents real challenges that would be naive to ignore.

A society where older people are increasingly numerous compared to the working population must rethink many balances: how to finance pensions, ensure care, and maintain solidarity between generations when those who work are proportionally fewer.
These questions are serious, and avoiding them would be irresponsible.
Aging requires reinventing a social organization designed for younger populations.
However, the way these challenges are framed is not neutral, and some discourses veer towards a troubling vision.

Presenting older people as a 'burden', pitting generations against each other, and reducing aging to a cost issue forgets that these older individuals have worked, contributed, and built the society that the younger ones benefit from, and that they continue to contribute a lot — through their experience, help, and presence.
A society that sees its elders only as a burden would be denying itself and preparing the fate it would one day reserve for those who today consider it a weight.
We must also guard against a catastrophism that presents aging as a fatality leading to decline.
Societies have always adapted to profound transformations, and nothing prevents us from thinking that they will be able to adapt to this one.
This requires choices — about work, solidarity, and the place of different ages — but these choices are possible.
Aging is only a disaster if we refuse to adapt to it; it can be experienced differently if we accept to rethink our ways of living together.
A society that is aging is therefore neither simply a success nor simply a crisis.
It is a major transformation, born of progress, carrying challenges, which calls for neither alarm nor denial, but for intelligence and justice.
The question is not whether we should rejoice or lament it, but how to make an older society one that remains just towards all its ages.

sentences: We like to think of ourselves as rational, judging things objectively.
The reality is more humble: our mind makes mistakes in regular, systematic, predictable ways.
These recurring errors, which research has patiently identified, are called biases.
They are not occasional faults, but deep-seated tendencies in our thinking that often operate without our awareness.
Becoming aware of them means discovering the blind spots in our own judgment.
One of the most powerful biases is the one that makes us seek out and retain what confirms our beliefs while neglecting what contradicts them.
We do not weigh evidence impartially; we readily accept the evidence that supports us and dismiss the evidence that disturbs us.
Thus, the more we believe something, the more reasons we find to believe it, not because there are more of them, but because we only see those.
This bias explains why it is so difficult to change someone's mind with facts: they do not see or reject contrary facts.
Another bias leads us to judge based on what easily comes to mind.
A striking, recent, spectacular event seems more frequent than it is, simply because it easily comes to our memory.
Thus, we overestimate the dangers that are widely discussed and underestimate those, sometimes greater, that are rarely mentioned.
Our perception of the world is distorted by what captures our imagination, not by what is actually probable.
This bias makes us poor judges of risks and manipulable by those who know what to highlight.

Other biases lead us to overestimate our own abilities, to judge in hindsight that we had 'foreseen everything,' to follow the group's opinion, and to give too much weight to the first information received.
The list is long, and what stands out is their systematic nature: these are not random errors, but regular distortions that all go in the same direction and are found in almost everyone.
Our mind is not a neutral instrument; it is equipped with tendencies that incline it, without our awareness, in predictable directions.
What makes these biases formidable is precisely that they operate without our awareness.
We do not feel that we are biased; we have the impression of judging objectively, even as our biases do their work.
Worse, we can much more easily spot the biases of others than our own: everyone sees the blindness of their neighbor and remains blind to their own.
This asymmetry is itself a bias and one of the most tenacious.
Believing that one is immune to biases is the best way to become their victim.
Can we correct ourselves?
Not entirely, because these biases are too deeply ingrained to be eliminated by sheer willpower.

But we can mitigate their effects: knowing of their existence, being wary of our overly confident judgments, deliberately seeking out what contradicts our views, and listening to those who think differently.
Above all, we can give up the illusion of our own objectivity, which is the first step towards a fairer judgment.
Recognizing that we have blind spots does not eliminate them, but it allows us to navigate with more caution — and that is already a lot.

sentences: There is an ancient distinction, at the heart of many wisdoms, whose simplicity hides depth: among the things that affect us, some depend on us, and others do not.
This distinction, which thinkers from Antiquity placed at the foundation of a good life, remains strikingly relevant.
For a large part of our suffering comes from the fact that we confuse them: we exhaust ourselves trying to change what does not depend on us, and neglect what does depend on us.
What depends on us?
Not external events, the behavior of others, the past, illness, death, the thousand circumstances that escape our will.
But our own judgments, our choices, our efforts, the way we react to what happens to us.
Here is the division: outside, a vast domain that we do not control; inside, a smaller but real domain, that of our attitude, which we can influence.
Wisdom begins by recognizing this boundary and ceasing to cross it in imagination.
For a major source of torment is wanting what does not depend on us.
We rebel against what is, we are consumed by an irreparable past, we want to control the uncontrollable, change others, bend events to our desires.
This struggle against the inevitable is lost from the start, and it exhausts us without changing anything.
You cannot bring back the dead, you cannot redo the past, you cannot force others to be what they are not.
Wanting these things is to condemn oneself to a sterile suffering.
Accepting what we cannot change is neither resignation nor passivity.
It is not giving up on acting, nor accepting everything with indifference.
It is to lucidly recognize the limits of our power, to concentrate our energy where it can make a difference, rather than wasting it where it cannot.
In the face of what does not depend on us, acceptance; in the face of what does depend on us, action and effort.
This distribution, far from weakening, makes us stronger: we stop fighting in vain, to act effectively where we have influence.
This wisdom applies even to the limits of existence.
There are evils that we cannot avoid, losses that we cannot repair, a finitude that we cannot abolish.
Against them, rebellion is futile, and acceptance, not bitter resignation but serene recognition, is the only path to peace.

Accepting that we cannot do everything, that we are mortal, vulnerable, dependent, is not a defeat; it is the condition for a peaceful existence, which has stopped fighting against reality to learn to live with it.
Distinguishing what depends on us from what does not is thus a key to a good life.

It frees us from two errors: the illusion of omnipotence, which wants to control everything and breaks against reality; and the feeling of powerlessness, which believes it can do nothing and gives up acting where it could.
Between the two, there is the right measure: to act with all our energy on what depends on us, to accept with serenity what does not.
A part of wisdom — and of peace — lies in this distinction, easy to state, difficult to live, but which illuminates an entire existence.

sentences: Today, it takes a certain kind of courage to embrace nuance.

In a public space divided into camps, where every issue seems to demand a binary choice, anyone who introduces a distinction, acknowledges a grain of truth in the opponent's position, and refuses to make a clear-cut decision as expected, exposes themselves to a double suspicion: being seen as lukewarm by some and as a traitor by others.
Nuance is often seen as an evasion, a lack of courage, a way of not choosing.
We must overturn this prejudice, because nuance, far from being cowardice, is one of the most demanding forms of intellectual courage.
First, let’s understand why nuance is so devalued.
In a polarized debate, the clarity of one’s camp outweighs the accuracy of the argument.
What is expected of you is not that you think correctly, but that you are clear: which side are you on?
Nuance muddles this clarity; it makes things uncertain, unclassifiable, and therefore suspect.
Those who embrace nuance do not provide the rallying cry that the group demands; they reject the simplification that allows for immediate identification of friends and enemies.
It is this rejection that is criticized, under the guise of blaming them for a lack of firmness.
However, to embrace nuance is not to hesitate or to refuse to conclude.

It is to recognize that reality is complex, that difficult questions involve contradictory considerations, that a position can be mostly correct while still having blind spots, and that the opponent can be mostly wrong while touching on some truth in one area.
Nuance is not the absence of conviction; it is conviction that has navigated complexity instead of fleeing from it.
It demands more, not less, than a clear-cut position: it requires holding together what polarization urges us to separate.
This is what makes it a form of courage.

It is easy and comfortable to unreservedly adopt your camp's position, to repeat its certainties, to share its indignations; you gain the approval of your peers, the feeling of belonging, and the relief from thinking for yourself.
Nuancing, on the contrary, means accepting to displease your own camp, exposing yourself to their reproach, and giving up the comfort of unreserved belonging.
It risks the solitude of someone who does not fully align, who maintains their freedom to judge against the pressure of the group.
This risk, many do not dare to take, and prefer the security of alignment to the discomfort of accuracy.
Moreover, nuance has a virtue that polarization destroys: it keeps the space for dialogue open.
Where clear-cut positions clash without meeting, nuance creates points of contact, acknowledges a part of reason in the other, and makes it possible to still listen to one another.
It is the opposite of a war between camps, not because it refuses to take sides, but because it takes sides without denying complexity or demonizing the opponent.
In this way, it may be the very condition for a debate that does not degenerate into confrontation — this fragile civilization that has been discussed.
Defending nuance is therefore not advocating for lukewarmness or refusing to engage.

It is a reminder that sound thinking embraces the complexity of its subject, that a solid conviction is not afraid to recognize its limitations, and that a fruitful debate requires minds capable of distinguishing rather than rallying.

In an era that rewards loud certainty and unreserved alignment, daring to embrace nuance, maintaining complexity against the pressure to simplify, and refusing to hate those we disagree with: this is what demands, today more than ever, true courage.
And perhaps it is this kind of courage, more than firmer convictions, that our debates lack the most.

sentences: People often confuse the past and history, as if history were just the past itself, faithfully reported.
This confusion leads to many misunderstandings, because the past and history are two distinct things.
The past is what was, the complete set of events, forever out of reach.
History is what we make of that past: the narrative we construct, the selection we make, the meaning we give it.
Distinguishing between the two is not a subtlety of scholars; it is understanding that history, far from being a mere reflection of the past, is always a construction of the present.
The past, in fact, is infinite and mute.
It does not tell itself; it is a chaos of countless events, the vast majority of which have not reached us and never will.
Making history means selecting, from this ocean, a few significant facts, ordering them, connecting them, and deriving a meaning.
However, this selection, this ordering, this meaning are not given in the past itself; they are the work of the historian, and behind him, of the era that supports him.
History always responds, in part, to questions posed by the present, and retains from the past what sheds light on those questions.
That is why history is constantly being rewritten, not out of whim, but out of necessity.
Each era interrogates the past based on its own concerns, discovering what previous ones had not seen, neglecting what had occupied them.
Entire sections of the past, long ignored — the history of women, the oppressed, the defeated, everyday life — have emerged as the present has become sensitive to these realities.
It is not that the past has changed; it is that the questions we ask of it have transformed.
History is a dialogue between the present and the past, and as the present changes, the dialogue is renewed.
Should we conclude that history would be arbitrary, that anyone could recount the past as they wish?
That would be a false and dangerous conclusion.
For if history is a construction, it is not a fiction: it is grounded in facts, constrained by traces, subject to methodological rules that distinguish serious history from novels or propaganda.
You cannot make the past say just anything; documents resist, facts oppose their objectivity, and a reconstruction that contradicts them is refutable.
History is a construction, but a rigorous construction, accountable to reality — which radically separates it from myth, which does not answer to any fact.
Understanding this nature of history has important consequences.
It invites vigilance towards any narrative of the past that presents itself as pure and simple truth, while it is always an interpretation, shaped by choices and values.
It also invites us to distinguish history, subject to criticism, from the political uses of the past, which instrumentalize it in service of a cause.

A nation, a power, a group can mobilize the past to legitimize themselves, but this mobilization is not history; it is militant memory, often necessary, but should not be confused with the critical work of the historian.

Distinguishing between the past and history, therefore, is both recognizing that our relationship to the past is always constructed, situated, revisable, and refusing to conclude that it would be arbitrary.
It is to hold together two truths: that history answers questions from the present, and that it remains accountable to the facts of the past.

This double awareness is characteristic of a mature relationship to history — one that does not take a narrative for definitive truth, but also does not fall into the idea that everything is equally valid.
The past will not return; but what we make of it, the history we write from it, engages who we are and who we want to be.

sentences: Among the most common reasoning errors, and the most consequential, is the confusion between correlation and causation.

Observing that two phenomena vary together — whether they increase or decrease in tandem — and concluding that one causes the other: this tempting shortcut is the source of countless false beliefs, erroneous decisions, and successful manipulations.
Understanding why correlation is not causation is one of the most valuable insights of rigorous thinking, and one of the most useful in everyday life.
The principle is simple to state.
That two things are correlated — that they occur together, vary in the same direction — does not establish that one is the cause of the other.
Three other explanations are always possible.
The causal relationship may be reversed: it is not A that causes B, but B that causes A.
A third factor may cause both at once, without them being directly related.
Or the correlation may be pure chance, a coincidence without significance.
In the face of any correlation, these possibilities must be ruled out before one can conclude causation, and this work is often difficult.
Examples abound, sometimes amusing, sometimes serious.

One might observe that in cities, the number of crimes increases with the number of police officers, and absurdly conclude that the police cause crime, when it is obviously crime that calls for more police: the causation is reversed.
One can observe that children with a rich vocabulary have larger feet, and imagine a link, while a third factor — age — explains both.
These examples seem obvious once stated, but the same error, in less clear cases, constantly deceives.
For in most real situations, the trap is much more subtle.

When we are presented with the idea that a certain behavior is correlated with a certain outcome — that those who do this live longer, that a certain product is associated with a certain disease — the temptation is strong to immediately conclude a cause, while the correlation could be explained by a thousand hidden factors.
Those who adopt such beneficial behavior may differ, in many other aspects, from those who do not adopt it, and it is these other differences that explain the outcome.
Untangling true causation from mere correlation requires rigorous methods, and a caution that spontaneous reasoning ignores.
This confusion is all the more dangerous because it is exploited.
Those who want to sell us a product, convince us of an idea, or make us adopt a behavior, readily wave correlations while presenting them as causalities.
"People who use this product are healthier": this statement suggests a causal link that the correlation does not prove, and that other factors could entirely explain.

Knowing how to resist these suggestions, systematically asking whether a presented correlation really establishes a cause, is an essential protection against manipulation by numbers and misinterpreted studies.
Remembering that correlation is not causation does not mean falling into a skepticism that would deny any causal link, as if one could never conclude anything.

It is to acquire a requirement: before concluding that one thing causes another, to rule out alternative explanations, to ask whether the link is real or apparent, to demand more than mere concomitance.
This requirement, which science has established as a method, is one of the most powerful tools of critical thinking.

In a world saturated with studies, statistics, and numbers brandished to convince us, knowing how to distinguish what varies together from what truly causes is now an indispensable skill — and one of the surest protections against credulity.

sentences: The human condition is made up of limits: we are mortal, vulnerable, dependent, ignorant of so many things, powerless in the face of so many others, and subject to the time that sweeps us away.
We can experience these limits in various ways, and our relationship to them shapes our wisdom or our misery.
At the end of these reflections on the tragic, the absurd, suffering, and defeat, a question arises that brings them together: how can we live with the human condition, with its irreducible limits?
Is it possible to find wisdom between the revolt that rejects them and the resignation that endures them?
The revolt against the human condition is a noble and understandable temptation.

To reject our limits, to refuse to resign ourselves to death, suffering, and powerlessness, to rebel against what weighs us down, there is a greatness in that, the greatness of the being who does not consent to their finitude, who demands more than what is given to them.
This revolt has inspired great things, the struggle against everything that can be fought, the refusal of everything that can be changed.
But when pushed to its limit, applied to what cannot be changed, it becomes futile and turns against the one who experiences it.

To rebel against death, against time, against finitude itself, is to condemn oneself to a fight that is lost from the start, to an added suffering on top of that of the condition, to a refusal that does not abolish what it rejects but poisons the relationship one has with it.
Resignation, on the other hand, consists of enduring the limits of the human condition, passively submitting to them, and renouncing any desire for fullness.
This attitude has its apparent wisdom: it avoids the suffering of futile revolt, it accepts what cannot be changed.
But it also has its cost: it is a form of anticipated death, a renunciation of life, a passivity that abdicates.
The resigned person no longer suffers from their limits because they have ceased to desire, ceased to hope, and in a sense, ceased to live fully.
Resignation buys peace at the cost of vitality; it extinguishes pain by extinguishing desire.
It is not wisdom, but its shadow, a false peace that resembles abdication.
Between futile revolt and dreary resignation, a third way may be possible, which we could call consent.
To consent is neither to rebel nor to resign; it is to accept the human condition, not passively, but actively, by saying yes to what is, including our limits, without renouncing living fully.

Consent recognizes our limits — death, finitude, vulnerability — it does not rebel against them as against an injustice, but neither does it resign itself to them as to a defeat; it integrates them, assumes them, and makes them the very condition of a fully lived life.
To consent to the human condition is to accept it as our own, with its limits, and to nonetheless deploy all the richness of existence, not despite these limits, but with them.
This consent is not easy, and it must not be confused with resignation, from which it profoundly differs.
The resigned person endures their limits by ceasing to live; the one who consents accepts them while living fully.
The difference lies in the inner attitude: consent is active, affirmative, it says yes to life within its limits, while resignation says no to desire to avoid suffering.
To consent to death is not to stop loving life; it is to love it all the more because we know it is finite.
To consent to vulnerability is not to renounce action; it is to act while knowing our limits.
To consent to the human condition is to embrace it entirely, its greatness and its limits, and to find, not despite it but through it, the possibility of a full life.
This wisdom of consent brings together what we have glimpsed.

It aligns with the wisdom regarding time, which loves what passes because it passes; that regarding suffering, which fights it without justifying it; that of the defeated, who finds greatness beyond success; and that of the tragic, which assumes the inevitable share of fault.

All converge towards this fundamental attitude: to accept the human condition in its limits, not through resignation, but through a consent that allows for fully living a finite, vulnerable, mortal existence.

Perhaps this is the highest wisdom that man can attain: not to abolish his limits, which is impossible, nor to resign himself to them, which is to die, but to consent to them while living fully — to make his finitude not a curse to flee from, but the very condition of a life that, because it is limited, deserves to be fully lived.

sentences: Reason is what humanity holds most precious, the instrument of its knowledge, science, and mastery of the world.
Celebrating reason, trusting it, and defending it against the irrational is a legitimate demand, and our era is right to cherish this legacy.
However, there is a higher form of rationality that consists of recognizing the limits of reason itself, knowing what it can and cannot do, and not asking it for more than it can give.
For it is still an act of reason to know one's own limits; and the most rigorous use of reason includes an awareness of what lies beyond its grasp.
Recognizing the limits of reason is not yielding to irrationalism, which belittles reason and prefers belief, feeling, and intuition.

Irrationalism is mistaken in devaluing reason; but excessive rationalism is also mistaken, attributing to it a power it does not possess, believing it can establish, demonstrate, and resolve everything.

Between the irrationalism that depreciates reason and the excessive rationalism that overestimates it, there is room for a more accurate position: one that acknowledges reason's immense power within its domain while recognizing that there are questions it cannot resolve, realities it cannot reach, and limits it cannot surpass.
What are these limits?

First, there are questions that do not fall under demonstrative reason, those we have encountered: questions of value, meaning, and purpose, which reason can illuminate but not resolve, as they cannot be deduced from any fact or indisputable principle.
Reason can tell us what is, not what ought to be; it can analyze means, not determine ultimate ends.
On these questions, reason is not powerless, but it cannot arrive at demonstrable conclusions; it illuminates the debate without closing it.
To claim that reason alone could establish what is just, good, or desirable is to ask it for more than it can provide.
Next, there are deeper limits that reason itself has discovered through self-examination.

Reflection on the foundations of knowledge, logic, and mathematics has revealed that reason cannot fully ground itself, that there are truths it cannot demonstrate, and internal limits to what it can establish.
The most rigorous reason has thus uncovered its own limits, not out of weakness, but through a deepening that has led it to recognize what it cannot reach.
These limits are not temporary failures that progress could overcome; they are principled limits, inherent to the very nature of reason.
Reason, in examining itself, has discovered that it cannot ground everything nor demonstrate everything.
Finally, there is the mystery, that which exceeds reason without contradicting it, before which it recognizes its inability to grasp.
We have encountered this mystery in aesthetic emotion, in the experience of the sublime, and in the question of the ultimate meaning of existence.
It is not about the irrational, which contradicts reason, but about the supra-rational, that which transcends it.
Reason can acknowledge that there are realities it cannot exhaust, experiences it cannot reduce, and dimensions of existence that exceed its grasp.
This recognition is not a defeat for reason, but its supreme clarity: knowing that there are more things in the world than reason can encompass.
Thus, recognizing the limits of reason is, paradoxically, the highest act of reason.

For it is the excessive reason, which believes itself all-powerful, that is in reality unreasonable, by failing to recognize its own limits; and it is the lucid reason, which knows what it can and cannot do, that is fully rational.
This clarity protects us from two extremes: the irrationalism that belittles reason, and the excessive rationalism that attributes unlimited power to it.
It invites us to fully utilize reason in its domain, where its authority is legitimate, while recognizing that there are questions, realities, and mysteries that surpass it.

Wisdom is neither renouncing reason nor demanding everything from it, but knowing it well enough to understand what to expect from it — and this knowledge of the limits of reason is itself the ripest fruit of its exercise.

sentences: We interact with others, talk to them, believe we know them; and yet, one troubling question remains: can we really know others?

Do we have access to what they truly are, to their inner life, to their consciousness, or do we only ever reach appearances, behaviors, words, never penetrating that core which essential solitude renders inaccessible?
This question, a continuation of the previous one, touches on the very possibility of knowing others, and thus on the nature of our most intimate relationships.
The problem is real and profound.
I only have direct access to my own consciousness; that of others is, by nature, inaccessible from the inside.
I perceive only their body, gestures, words, expressions; their inner life, thoughts, feelings, I only know indirectly, through what they show and what I infer.
I can never verify that what I infer about their inner self corresponds to what they actually feel; there remains, between their consciousness and mine, a distance that nothing quite crosses.
In a rigorous sense, I never know others directly; I interpret them, I guess them, I reconstruct them based on what they allow me to perceive.

This difficulty has fostered skepticism about knowing others: we would be forever trapped in our own consciousness, unable to reach that of others, condemned to know only appearances behind which the inner life of others would remain forever hidden.
This position has its logical strength, but it clashes with our experience.
For we do indeed have the feeling of knowing certain beings, of understanding them, of guessing what they feel, sometimes better than they understand themselves.
Is this feeling illusory?
Or do we really reach others, despite the impossibility of direct access to their consciousness?
Perhaps we must acknowledge that knowing others, while not being impossible direct access to their consciousness, is nonetheless real, of a different nature.
We do not know others as we know ourselves, from the inside; but we know them in our own way, through meeting, frequenting, paying attention, and empathy.

By continually being around a being, observing them, communicating with them, putting ourselves in their shoes, we acquire knowledge of them that, while not access to their consciousness, is nonetheless real and sometimes profound.
This knowledge consists of interpretation, inference, and empathy; it remains fallible, uncertain, never complete; but it reaches something of the other, it is not pure illusion.
We know others not by entering their consciousness, but by meeting them, interpreting them accurately, and opening ourselves to them.
We must nonetheless recognize the limits of this knowledge, and guard against the illusion of knowing others entirely.

For even the closest, best-known being retains a part of mystery, unpredictability, and unfathomability; we never exhaust them, they can always surprise us, escape us, reveal themselves to be different from what we believed.
This irreducible part of mystery in others is not just a limit of our knowledge; it is the respect owed to their freedom, their uniqueness, and their essential solitude.

To claim to know others entirely, to confine them to the idea we have of them, is in a sense to do violence to them, denying their freedom to surprise us, their capacity to change, their inexhaustible depth.
The just knowledge of others includes the recognition of what they keep unknowable.
This conception has an ethical dimension.

For knowing others, in this respect for their mystery, is also a way of treating them justly: not to confine them to a fixed image, to remain open to what they can reveal to us, to approach them with the humility of someone who knows they never fully know them.
The worst way to treat others is to believe we know them inside and out, to reduce them to the idea we have of them, to deny their depth and freedom.

The just knowledge of others is one that seeks to understand them while respecting their mystery, that interprets them accurately while remaining open to seeing them differently, that truly reaches them while recognizing it never exhausts them.

In essence, knowing others is not about piercing their secret, but about maintaining a relationship with them where understanding and respect for the mystery come together — where we approach them without ever claiming to possess them entirely.

sentences: When I started my current job six years ago, I understood almost nothing.
The company was using software that I didn't know.
There were rules, words that everyone understood except me.
During meetings, I took notes, but I didn't ask any questions.
I was afraid of looking stupid.
In the evening, I would go home worried.
I thought, 'They made a mistake hiring me.'
After two weeks, a colleague came to talk to me.
His name was Bernard.
He had been working there for twenty-two years and he was almost sixty.
'How are you?' he asked me.
'You look lost.'
I hesitated, then I told the truth: "I don't understand half of what people say to me."
He laughed kindly.
"Of course!
No one understands at the beginning.
Not me either, in 2002."
From that day on, Bernard took fifteen minutes every morning to explain things to me.
He told me a phrase that I haven't forgotten: "The stupid question is the one you don't ask."
Bernard retired last year.
Last month, a young woman joined my team.
She looked lost in the meeting.
I went to see her.
How are you?
Do you want us to take fifteen minutes tomorrow morning?

sentences: For three weeks, my upstairs neighbor made a lot of noise.
Every evening, between ten PM and midnight, I heard music and heavy footsteps.
I was sleeping poorly.
In the morning, I was tired at work.
At first, I didn't say anything.
I hoped it would stop on its own.
Then I became really angry.
I thought about writing an anonymous note, or even calling the police.
My colleague Aïcha gave me some advice: "Go talk to him first.
Most people don't know they are bothering others."
She was surely right, but I was scared.
One Saturday morning, I gathered my courage and went upstairs to knock on his door.
He opened the door.
He looked surprised and a bit worried.
I explained calmly, "Hello, I live just below.
I hear a lot of noise in the evening and I sleep poorly."
His reaction surprised me.
He turned completely red.
"I'm really sorry!
I just moved in and I exercise in the evening after work.
I didn't think it could be heard."
We talked for ten minutes.
He suggested a thick carpet and finishing before ten o'clock.
Since then, there's almost no noise.
Three weeks of anger, and it only took ten minutes.

sentences: Every language names certain things and leaves others unsaid; it illuminates some areas of experience while leaving others in the dark, due to a lack of words to express them.
This silence of language, these experiences that our language does not name, raise a troubling question: does what has no name exist for us?
Does the absence of a word condemn an experience to non-existence, or does it persist, silent, waiting for the word that will reveal it?
This question, an extension of our previous reflections, touches on the most intimate relationships between language, perception, and being.
It is certain that language guides our attention, and that what it names, we perceive better.

A language that distinguishes several shades of a color, several states of an emotion, and several forms of a human relationship with specific words makes its speakers more attentive to these distinctions; conversely, what a language does not name tends to go unnoticed, blending into the indistinct.
The word, by naming, carves out experience, makes it stand out, and brings it into existence as an object of attention.
What our language does not name thus risks remaining below our conscious perception, not because it does not exist, but because nothing designates it, detaches it, or makes it noticeable.
But should we conclude that what has no name does not exist at all for us?
That would be going too far.

For we often experience things that we cannot name, confused emotions, vague perceptions, states that have no word in our language and yet are there, obscurely present, demanding a name that they do not yet have.

This experience of the unnamed — this feeling of experiencing something for which words are lacking — proves that experience can precede the word, that it exists before being named, even in the shadows of consciousness.
What has no name is therefore not nothing; it is what awaits its name, what exists in the realm of the obscure, the confused, the formless, before the word comes to reveal and articulate it.
It is here that the creative power of language is revealed.

For naming an experience that has hitherto been unnamed is not just labeling it; it is bringing it fully into existence, pulling it out of the shadows, constituting it as an object of consciousness and thought.
When a new word comes to name an experience that everyone felt but could not express, something happens: this experience, suddenly named, stands out, becomes recognizable, shareable, thinkable.
The word does not create the experience out of nothing; rather, it fulfills it, moving it from the obscure to the clear, from the private to the shared, from the sensed to the conceived.

That is why the creation of missing words is an act of immense significance: it gives full existence to what existed only partially, it makes what everyone felt in the solitude of the unnamed expressible and therefore shareable.
This revealing function of language has an ethical and political dimension that we would be wrong to overlook.

For there are sufferings, injustices, and experiences that, lacking words to name them, remain invisible, unspeakable, condemned to silence; those who endure them feel them without being able to express, denounce, or have them recognized.
To forge the word that names them is to make them exist in the common space, allowing them to be recognized and fought against.
Many struggles have begun with the conquest of a word, through the naming of a reality that the absence of a name kept in the shadows.
The silence of what has no name is not always innocent; it can be the silence imposed on what we prefer not to see, and giving it a name is then an act of justice.
Thus, what has no name occupies a singular status: neither fully existing for us nor entirely nonexistent, it lingers in the twilight of the unnamed, demanding the word that will fulfill it.
Language does not create experience out of nothing, but it reveals it, constitutes it, and brings it from the obscure to the clear.

That is why enriching a language, forging the missing words, and learning the words of another language for what one's own does not express is not just a simple vocabulary game: it is about expanding the realm of the sayable, and therefore of the thinkable, shareable, and existent.

Every word conquered from silence is a region of experience torn from the shadows — and one who learns a new language does not just gain words, but entire sections of a world that their mother tongue perhaps left in the silence of the unnamed.
