sentences: A tension runs through modern moral and political thought, which globalization has made more acute: the one between universalism and respect for cultural diversity.
On one hand, the idea that there are universal values, valid for all people everywhere — human rights, human dignity, certain principles of justice — that no culture can legitimately violate.
On the other hand, respect for cultural diversity, for their own values, for their right to be different, against the claim to impose a single model on them.
These two demands, equally respectable, seem to oppose each other; and their conflict is one of the most challenging of our time.
Universalism asserts that there are values valid for all, regardless of cultures, and that in the name of these values, one can judge cultures, condemning their practices when they violate them.

This position has its strength and nobility: it refuses to allow anything in the name of culture, it affirms a dignity of man that no tradition can legitimately violate, it establishes the possibility of condemning oppression, cruelty, and injustice, wherever they occur.
Without universalism, nothing could be condemned in any culture, everything would have to be accepted in the name of diversity, including the unacceptable.
Universalism is what allows us to say that certain practices are unjust, regardless of the culture that permits them.
But universalism also has its dangers, which the respect for diversity highlights.
For the claim to universality can mask the imposition of a particular culture, wrongly presented as universal.

What we consider to be universal values may only be the values of a dominant culture, imposed on others in the name of the universal, in a gesture that has justified domination, colonization, and the erasure of cultures in the name of a universal that was actually particular.
Universalism can be a disguised imperialism, a way of imposing one's culture while passing it off as humanity itself.

Respect for diversity reminds us of this truth: that cultures have their own value, their legitimacy, their right to difference, and that pretending to judge them in the name of the universal can be an arrogance.
How can we move beyond this opposition?
Neither absolute universalism, which would deny any legitimacy to diversity, nor absolute relativism, which would prohibit any judgment, are tenable.
The former leads to the imposition of a single model, to the erasure of differences, to the arrogance that takes its particular for the universal.
The latter leads to the acceptance of everything in the name of culture, to the impossibility of condemning the unacceptable, to a respect for diversity that becomes complicity in oppression.
Between these two dead ends, we must seek a path that recognizes both the existence of some truly universal values and the legitimacy of cultural diversity.

This path may involve a distinction: between a small number of truly universal values, which relate to the fundamental dignity of man and which no culture can legitimately violate, and the immense diversity of ways of living, customs, and secondary values, which pertain to the legitimate differences among cultures.

Thus, there would be a universal core, limited but firm — the prohibition of cruelty, respect for dignity, certain fundamental rights — and, beyond that, a vast realm of legitimate diversity, where cultures can and must differ.

This distinction allows for the condemnation of the unacceptable without imposing a single model, for respecting diversity without accepting everything, and for holding together the universalist demand and respect for differences.
Such a position is not easy to maintain, as the boundary between the universal core and the realm of diversity is difficult to draw and is itself the subject of debate.

But it points to the direction of wisdom: neither the universalist arrogance that imposes its particularity, nor the relativism that renounces all judgment, but the recognition of a restricted and firm universal, combined with respect for legitimate diversity.

This position perhaps aligns with the best of what France has in its universalism when it remains clear-sighted: not the pretension to impose its culture in the name of humanity, but fidelity to a few truly universal values, joined with respect for the diversity of ways of being human.

Believing in the universal without imposing its particularity, respecting diversity without renouncing all judgment: this is the difficult balance that our time demands, where cultures coexist as never before, and where we must learn to defend what is valid for all while respecting what legitimately differs.

sentences: Among the qualities that contribute to a wise and happy life, there is one that is rarely discussed yet profoundly transforms existence: gratitude.

Not the simple politeness of saying thank you, but a deeper disposition, one that involves recognizing what is given to us, perceiving and appreciating the goods of our existence, rather than obsessing over what we lack.
This disposition, which can be cultivated, has a transformative power that we underestimate, and it deserves a place in any reflection on wisdom and the art of living.
Our natural inclination leads us away from gratitude: to desire what we do not have rather than to appreciate what we do have, to focus on what we lack instead of what is given to us.

We quickly become accustomed to our possessions, which cease to bring us joy, while our desires are always directed towards what we are missing; we live in perpetual lack, dissatisfied with what we have, reaching for what we do not have.

This disposition towards dissatisfaction, fueled by habituation and by a society that constantly stirs up new desires, prevents us from enjoying what is given to us, keeping us in a lack that nothing fills.
We have much, yet we continually feel the absence of what we do not have.
Gratitude reverses this disposition.
It involves directing our attention not to what is lacking, but to what is given; to perceive, recognize, and appreciate the goods of our existence that habituation makes us forget.
It helps us see what we no longer notice due to our familiarity: health when we have it, the presence of those we love, the goods we enjoy, the beauty of the world, the simple fact of existing.
Gratitude is this attention to what is given to us, this ability to rejoice in it, to recognize it as a good, instead of taking it for granted and obsessing over what is lacking.
It is a shift in perspective, turning towards the abundance of what is given rather than the emptiness of what is missing.
This shift profoundly transforms the quality of life.

For the one who cultivates gratitude lives in a world different from that of the one who lives in lack: where the dissatisfied sees only what he lacks, the grateful perceives the abundance of what is given to him; where one lives in frustration, the other lives in appreciation.
Gratitude does not change external circumstances; it changes the relationship we have with them, and thereby, profoundly, our experience of life.
It is one of the keys to that contentment which does not depend on what we have, but on how we look at it.
The same fate can be experienced in frustration or in gratitude, and this difference in perspective makes all the difference in happiness.
Gratitude also has a dimension that goes beyond mere well-being, an almost metaphysical depth.

For recognizing what is given to us is to acknowledge that we are not the source of all that we enjoy, that much has been given to us without us having earned or produced it: life itself, the world, those who have shaped us, all this heritage that we did not create.

Gratitude is the acknowledgment of this debt, of what we owe to what precedes and transcends us; it is a form of humility, which recognizes that we do not owe everything to ourselves, that our existence is supported by what has been given to us.
In this sense, gratitude is more than a technique for happiness; it is a truth about our condition as beings who receive more than they produce, who owe to others and to the world what they enjoy.
Cultivating gratitude is therefore an essential part of wisdom.

It’s not about denying what is lacking, the evils, the trials, which are real; nor about settling for a naive optimism that refuses to see the bad; but rather learning to also perceive, and first and foremost, what is given, to rejoice in it, and to acknowledge it.

This disposition, which is cultivated through attention, through the habit of recognizing the goods of one’s existence, transforms the quality of life; it is one of the paths to a contentment that does not depend on circumstances, but on the perspective one has on them.

In a world that heightens the sense of lack, that focuses us on what we do not have, cultivating gratitude, learning to recognize and appreciate what is given to us, is an act of wisdom and almost of resistance — and perhaps one of the keys to a life that, without denying its lacks and trials, still knows how to rejoice in what it has received.

sentences: Every summer, there is a tennis tournament in Julien's neighborhood.
This year, Julien decides to participate.
It's his first time.
He doesn't play tennis very often.
But he likes to try new things.
The tournament starts on a Saturday morning.
There are twenty players.
Julien plays against a man older than him.
The man's name is Marc.
Marc plays very well.
He easily wins the first set.
Julien tries, but he loses the match.
Three sets to zero.
"It's okay," says Marc after the match.
"You played well for a beginner."
Julien is not sad.
He had a good time.
"The important thing is not to win," he says to Yanis.
"It's to play and have fun."
Next year, Julien wants to participate again.
Maybe he will win a match this time.

sentences: The small cinema in my neighborhood closed its doors last month, after forty years.
It was an independent cinema, with only two screens.
I had been going there since my childhood.
The owner, Mr. Lenoir, opened it with his father in nineteen eighty-five.
His whole life was tied to this cinema.
In recent years, fewer and fewer people came.
Many preferred to watch movies at home, on a streaming platform.
"We can no longer pay the rent with so few spectators," Mr. Lenoir explained in an interview.
The last screening took place on a Sunday evening.

He fixed the pipe in just twenty minutes, with the right tools.
It's not a big deal, he told me with a smile.

sentences: For the past few months, I've noticed that I've been spending a lot more money than before on online shopping.
In the evening, while looking at my phone before going to sleep, I often received notifications about promotions.
These messages always announced a limited offer: 'Only three hours left to take advantage of this discount!'
Without really thinking, I clicked and bought, almost reflexively.
When I looked at my bank statement at the end of the month, I discovered that I had spent much more than I thought, on small purchases I had almost forgotten.
A friend explained to me that these sites are designed exactly to create this sense of urgency.
'They want you to buy without thinking, before you change your mind,' she told me.
I decided to change my habits.
Now, when I see something I want to buy, I wait twenty-four hours before confirming my order.
Most of the time, after this delay, I no longer really want that item.
I also disabled the notifications from these sites on my phone.
This small change has allowed me to save a lot of money and regain control over my purchases.

sentences: For the past two years, I have stopped eating meat.
My family has not always accepted this choice well.
My decision was mainly due to environmental concerns, after reading several articles about the impact of livestock on the climate.
At the first family meal after my change, my grandmother seemed almost offended.
"Do you no longer like my cooking?" she asked me, a bit hurt by what she perceived as a rejection.
I had to explain, patiently and several times, that this choice had nothing to do with her cooking, which I still loved just as much, but simply with my own personal beliefs.
My brother, on the other hand, reacted differently, almost with annoyance.
He thinks that I unnecessarily complicate family meals by forcing everyone to plan an alternative for me.
Over time, the situation has calmed down.
My grandmother has even learned a few vegetarian recipes that she now happily prepares for me.
My brother still finds it a bit inconvenient, but he has eventually accepted this difference without commenting on it at every meal.
One of my nephews, without me ever asking him to, ended up following the same path, simply by observing my choices during our shared meals.
This discreet influence, never claimed, seemed to me ultimately more effective than any argument I could have made directly at the table.
This experience showed me that a personal food choice can touch, much more than one might imagine, sensitive family issues related to tradition and belonging.

sentences: When I was looking for a new apartment last year, I discovered how difficult it was to find a place that accepted my dog.
Out of about twenty listings that interested me, almost half clearly stated: 'no pets allowed.'
Some landlords, contacted directly, categorically refused to discuss it, despite my explanations about my dog's calm behavior.
This situation seemed unfair to me.
My dog, an eight-year-old Labrador, has never caused any damage in my previous apartment, where I lived for five years without any problems.
A lawyer friend explained to me that the law in my country actually protects tenants with small pets, but many landlords still continue to enforce their own rules, which is illegal.
This discovery prompted me to better inform myself about my rights before my next search.
I finally found an apartment that welcomed my dog, after several discouraging weeks of searching.
Some organizations now offer labels indicating which homes are truly pet-friendly, which makes it easier for other tenants in my situation to find a place.
This type of initiative, still little known, deserves more visibility since the difficulty I encountered seems widely shared around me.

This experience made me think about a broader question: in a society where more and more people live alone with a pet for company, shouldn't we rethink some housing rules that have, in my opinion, become outdated?

sentences: For a long time, video games were considered a mere minor entertainment, unworthy of being compared to forms of art traditionally recognized such as literature, cinema, or painting.
This cultural hierarchy seems increasingly contested today.

Several major museums around the world have recently dedicated entire exhibitions to the history and aesthetics of video games, explicitly recognizing their artistic value and legitimate place in contemporary cultural history.

The arguments in favor of this recognition are based on substantial elements: some modern games deploy narratives of a narrative complexity comparable to the best literary works, a visual artistic direction of remarkable sophistication, and above all, an interactive dimension unique to this medium, allowing the player to actively participate in constructing the meaning of the work, a possibility that no other traditional artistic form offers in the same way.

Skeptics retort that this recent recognition mainly concerns a minority of particularly ambitious productions, while the vast majority of commercial video games are primarily designed to maximize entertainment and profit, without any real artistic pretension.

This objection is not without foundation, but it could equally apply to other artistic forms: cinema also has a majority of purely commercial productions, without this calling into question the artistic status of the medium as a whole.

Video games thus seem to be undergoing a transition today comparable to that experienced by cinema in the twentieth century: from a popular entertainment despised by the cultural establishment to a gradual recognition of its own artistic potential, specific and irreducible to that of the mediums that preceded it.

sentences: It is not a cry of disbelief, but at least it is a cry of skepticism.
Undoubtedly, it is difficult to understand and believe, but why this astonishment that arises at death?
Why?
Because this occurrence is something that is a mystery, because it is hard to understand and judge, but one must resign oneself to it.

And I say that if death is the arrival of nothingness, if the blissful husband feels his love grow upon learning of his wife's affairs, if opinion is represented by one of the grotesque beings, if religious sentiment is represented by a ridiculous priest, only one person is right, reigns, dominates: it is Emma Bovary; Messalina is right against Juvenal.
Here is the philosophical conclusion of the book, drawn not by the author, but by a man who reflects and delves into things, by a man who sought in the book a character who could dominate this woman.
There isn't one.
The only character who dominates is Mrs. Bovary.
One must therefore look elsewhere than in the book; one must look in this Christian morality that is the foundation of modern civilizations.
For this morality, everything is explained and clarified.

sentences: A question arose in my mind.
How did the commander of this floating dwelling operate?
Did he obtain air through chemical means, by releasing oxygen contained in potassium chlorate through heat, and absorbing carbon dioxide with caustic potash?
In that case, he must have maintained some connections with the continents to procure the necessary materials for this operation.
Was he merely storing air under high pressure in tanks, then releasing it according to the needs of his crew?
Perhaps.
Or, in a more convenient, economical, and therefore more likely method, did he simply come up to the surface to breathe, like a cetacean, and renew his supply of atmosphere for twenty-four hours?
In any case, regardless of the method, it seemed wise to employ it without delay.
Indeed, I had already been forced to take deep breaths to extract the little oxygen that cell contained when, suddenly, I was refreshed by a current of pure air, fragrant with salty emanations.
It was indeed the sea breeze, invigorating and rich in iodine!
I opened my mouth wide, and my lungs filled with fresh molecules.
At the same time, I felt a swaying, a roll of moderate amplitude, but perfectly discernible.
The boat, the metal monster, had obviously just come back to the surface of the Ocean to breathe like whales do.
The ship's ventilation system was therefore perfectly recognized.
When I had inhaled this pure air deeply, I looked for the duct, the 'air duct', if you will, that allowed this beneficial breeze to reach us, and I soon found it.
Above the door, there was an air vent letting in a fresh column of air, which thus renewed the depleted atmosphere of the cell.

sentences: They were at the Hôtel de Boulogne, by the port.
And they lived there, with the shutters closed, doors locked, flowers on the ground, and ice syrups brought to them first thing in the morning.
In the evening, they would take a covered boat and go to dinner on an island.
It was the time when one could hear, by the shipyards, the sound of the carpenters' mallets striking the hulls of the vessels.
The smoke from the tar was rising among the trees, and on the river, large, thick drops were seen, undulating unevenly under the purple light of the sun, like floating plates of Florentine bronze.
They descended among the moored boats, whose long, slanting cables brushed lightly against the top of their boat.
The sounds of the city gradually faded away: the rumble of carts, the tumult of voices, the barking of dogs on the decks of the ships.
She untied her hat, and they landed on their island.
They settled in the lower room of a tavern, which had black nets hanging at its door.
They ate fried smelts, cream, and cherries.

They lay on the grass; they kissed discreetly under the poplars; and they wished, like two Robinsons, to live forever in this little place, which seemed to them, in their bliss, the most magnificent on earth.

It was not the first time they had seen trees, blue sky, grass, heard the water flowing and the breeze blowing through the leaves; but they had undoubtedly never admired all of this as if nature had not existed before, or that it had only begun to be beautiful since the fulfillment of their desires.
As night fell, they set off again.
The boat followed the edge of the islands.
They remained at the back, both hidden in the shadows, without speaking.
The square oars sounded against the iron thole pins; and this marked the silence like a metronome, while at the back the dragging stern continued its gentle lapping in the water.
Once, the moon appeared; then they couldn't help but make phrases, finding the celestial body melancholic and full of poetry; she even began to sing:

sentences: I approached this phenomenal mollusk.
By its byssus, it was adhering to a granite table, and there it was developing in isolation in the calm waters of the cave.
I estimated the weight of this tridacna to be three hundred kilograms.
Now, such an oyster contains fifteen kilos of flesh, and it would take the stomach of a Gargantua to absorb a few dozen.
Captain Nemo was obviously aware of the existence of this bivalve.
It wasn't the first time he had visited it, and I thought that by bringing us to this place, he only wanted to show us a natural curiosity.
I was mistaken.
Captain Nemo had a particular interest in observing the current state of this tridacna.
The two valves of the mollusk were slightly open.
The captain approached and inserted his dagger between the shells to prevent them from closing; then, with his hand, he lifted the membranous and fringed tunic that formed the mantle of the animal.
There, among the leafy folds, I saw a free pearl the size of a coconut.
Its globular shape, perfect clarity, and admirable luster made it a jewel of inestimable value.
Driven by curiosity, I reached out to grab it, to weigh it, to feel it!
But the captain stopped me, shook his head, and, quickly drawing his dagger, he let the two shells close suddenly.
I then understood what Captain Nemo's plan was.
By leaving this pearl buried under the mantle of the tridacna, he allowed it to grow gradually.
With each passing year, the secretion of the mollusk added new concentric layers.
Only the captain knew the cave where this marvelous fruit of nature was 'ripening'; he alone nurtured it, so to speak, in order to one day transport it to his precious museum.

Perhaps, following the example of the Chinese and Indians, he had initiated the production of this pearl by introducing some piece of glass and metal under the folds of the mollusk, which had gradually been covered with the nacreous material.
In any case, comparing this pearl to those I already knew, to those that shone in the captain's collection, I estimated its value at least at ten million francs.
A superb natural curiosity and not a luxury jewel, for I don't know what feminine ears could have borne it.

sentences: The whole crowd applauded this proposal, and thought only of sacrificing us.

They were already leading us to the tomb of Anchises; two altars had been set up there, where the sacred fire was lit; the sword that was to pierce us was before our eyes; we had been crowned with flowers, and no compassion could guarantee our lives; it was all over for us when Mentor calmly asked to speak to the king.
He said to him:
O Acestes, if the misfortune of young Telemachus, who has never borne arms against the Trojans, cannot touch you, at least let your own interest touch you.

The knowledge I have gained of omens and the will of the gods tells me that before three days have passed, you will be attacked by barbarian peoples, who come like a torrent from the heights of the mountains, to flood your city and ravage your entire land.
Be quick to prevent them; put your people under arms, and do not waste a moment to bring back within your walls the rich herds you have in the countryside.
If my prediction is false, you will be free to sacrifice us in three days; if, on the contrary, it is true, remember that one should not take the life of those from whom one receives it.
Aceste was astonished by these words, which Mentor spoke to him with a confidence he had never found in any man.
I can see well, he replied, oh stranger, that the gods, who have dealt so poorly with you in all the gifts of fortune, have granted you a wisdom that is more valuable than all prosperity.
At the same time, he delayed the sacrifice and diligently gave the necessary orders to prevent the attack that Mentor had threatened him with.
All around, there were only trembling women, bent old men, little children with tears in their eyes, who were retreating into the city.
The lowing oxen and bleating sheep came in crowds, leaving the lush pastures, and could not find enough barns to take shelter.

There were, from all sides, confused cries of people pushing against one another, who could not hear each other, who mistook a stranger for their friend in the chaos, and who ran without knowing where their steps were leading.
But the leaders of the city, believing themselves to be wiser than the others, imagined that Mentor was a fraud who had made a false prediction to save his life.

sentences: On Sunday mornings, in many French towns, there is a market.
People go there to buy fruits, vegetables, cheese, and bread.
But the market is not just a place to do grocery shopping.
It's also a meeting place.
You run into your neighbors, chat, and take your time.
The products are often fresher than in the supermarket.
Many come from farms close to the city.
The sellers know their products and are happy to give advice.
"Try this tomato," says a seller.
"It comes from my garden."
Of course, the market can sometimes be a bit more expensive.
But for many people, the atmosphere is worth that little price.
After the market, some people go to have a coffee on the terrace.
It's a nice way to start the weekend.

sentences: When you turn on the tap, water flows effortlessly, and it's easy to forget that it's a limited resource.
Across the planet, freshwater, the kind we can drink, makes up a very small part of all the water that exists.
For a long time, in wealthy countries, this resource was considered almost infinite.
But things are changing.
Droughts are becoming more frequent, and some regions run out of water at certain times of the year.
Agriculture, industry, and cities consume enormous amounts of it.
It wouldn't be reasonable to continue as if nothing were happening.
Reducing waste is possible at all levels: fixing leaks, watering less, choosing crops suited to the climate.
There is still time to act, but only if we take the problem seriously right now.
Water seems ordinary precisely because it is essential; perhaps that's why we protect it too little.

sentences: There was a time when cities competed for tourists, seeing them as a source of prosperity.
Today, some of them complain, on the contrary, about having too many.
Residents are protesting against the influx of visitors, municipalities are trying to limit it, and a new word has emerged to describe this phenomenon: "overtourism."

This reversal, seemingly paradoxical, reveals a reality that tourist enthusiasm had long masked: beyond a certain threshold, tourism stops benefiting the places that host it and starts to destroy them.
The effects of this saturation are concrete.
In the most visited cities, housing is being transformed into accommodations for tourists, pushing residents out due to rising rents.
Local shops are giving way to souvenir stores.
The streets, overcrowded, become impassable for those who live there.
Little by little, the city is emptying of its residents and its own life, turning into a backdrop for passing visitors.
It survives economically, but dies as a place to live.
The paradox is that this process ultimately ruins what attracted visitors.
People come to these cities for their charm, authenticity, and unique life; but the very influx of visitors destroys that charm and life.
In the end, all that remains is a shell, perhaps beautiful, but emptied of its substance — a place that one visits without being able to encounter anything other than other visitors.
Why is this problem so difficult to solve?
Because tourism is profitable, and the interests that depend on it are powerful.
Limiting the number of visitors means giving up immediate revenue, which few are willing to do.
Moreover, each stakeholder, taken individually, has an interest in benefiting from the windfall, even if it harms the whole.
No visitor feels responsible for a saturation to which they believe they contribute only in a minimal way.
Solutions do exist, even if they face these resistances: limiting the number of visitors, regulating tourist accommodations, protecting residents' housing, and distributing flows over time and space.
None of them is simple; all require prioritizing the interests of the places and those who live there over immediate profit.
Overtourism, at its core, holds up a mirror to us.
It shows what happens when a place is treated as just a resource to exploit, without regard for those who live there.
And it reminds us of a truth that travelers often forget: the places we love to visit are primarily the homes of others.

sentences: In the face of the ecological crisis, a hope keeps resurfacing, appealing in its convenience: technology will save us.
Innovation, it is said, will find solutions — clean energies, efficient processes, inventions that will allow us to preserve the planet without giving up our way of life.
This techno-optimistic hope is powerful because it spares us from painful changes: there is no need to transform our lives, we just have to wait for human ingenuity to solve the problem.
But this hope deserves critical examination, as it mixes a grain of truth with a dangerous illusion.
Let's start with the grain of truth, as it would be absurd to disdain technology.
Innovation has a crucial role to play in responding to the ecological crisis, and claiming otherwise would be a mere posture.
New techniques — in energy, agriculture, industry — can significantly reduce our footprint, allow us to do more with less, and open up possibilities that no mere renunciation could provide.
Refusing by principle to resort to technology, in the name of a return to an idealized previous state, would be both unrealistic and counterproductive.
Technology is part of the solution, and it needs to be developed.
However, techno-optimistic hope becomes an illusion when it turns into a passive waiting for a miraculous solution that would exempt us from any change.
This illusion contains several errors.

The first is to take for granted that technology will find the necessary solutions in time, whereas nothing guarantees this: betting our entire future on hypothetical innovations, which may not arrive or may come too late, is an unwise gamble.
Hoping that technology will save us is not a strategy; it is a wish that relieves us from acting while waiting for an uncertain salvation.
The second error is to ignore that technology, while solving certain problems, often creates others.
History shows that technical solutions frequently have unforeseen perverse effects, shifting problems rather than eliminating them, generating new difficulties as they resolve old ones.
Relying on technology to solve everything forgets that it is, in part, the source of the problems we ask it to address, and that it could create new ones.
Blind faith in technology overlooks this ambivalence.
The third mistake, the most subtle, is that techno-optimistic hope often serves as an excuse for inaction and the maintenance of the existing order.
By promising that technology will preserve our way of life without us having to change it, it reassures, lulls, and absolves us from questioning what should be questioned.
It allows those who benefit from the current order to defend it, indefinitely postponing change in the name of a future technical salvation.
Thus, "technology will solve the problem" becomes a way of doing nothing, of continuing as before, of refusing necessary transformations.
Technical optimism, beneath its dynamic facade, can be the most effective form of conservatism.
The correct position is therefore neither the techno-optimism that expects everything from technology, nor the technophobic rejection that expects nothing from it.
It is about recognizing that technology is an essential means, but one means among others, which will not exempt us from changes in behavior, organization, and way of life.

Yes, we should develop useful technologies; but without using them as an excuse to change nothing else, without betting our future on hypothetical solutions, without forgetting that technology itself must be guided by choices.
Technology will not save us on its own; it can help us, if we also do the rest.
And it is precisely this "rest" — the changes that techno-optimistic hope invites us to evade — that is the most difficult and the most necessary.

sentences: Increasingly, systems are making decisions for us.
They choose our path, recommend what we should watch, read, buy, and sometimes even who we should meet; they guide medical, financial, and administrative decisions.
Often, they decide better than we would: faster, with more data, and fewer errors.
This growing delegation of our decisions to systems therefore appears as progress, and it is in many ways.
But it raises a question that its very effectiveness makes us forget: what happens to our judgment when we stop exercising it?
We must first recognize the real benefits of this delegation.
In many areas, the systems that decide for us spare us from mistakes, effort, and wasted time.
They process vast amounts of information that we could not grasp, identify patterns that escape us, and avoid biases that distort our judgments.

Refusing these aids on principle, in the name of an autonomy of decision elevated to an absolute, would be unreasonable: there are decisions where it is better to rely on a reliable system than on our own fallible judgment.
Delegation is not inherently a bad thing.
But judgment, like any ability, is maintained through practice and atrophies through idleness.
As we delegate our decisions, we stop exercising the ability to decide, and this ability, due to lack of use, weakens.
We lose the habit of weighing options, choosing, and taking responsibility; we rely on others, and by relying on them, we become unable to do otherwise.

What starts as a convenience — letting the system decide because it decides better — ends up as a dependency: we no longer know how to decide without it, we have unlearned the judgment we stopped exercising.
Help has become a crutch that we can no longer do without.
This atrophy of judgment is all the more concerning as it makes us vulnerable.
For the systems to which we delegate are not infallible, nor are they disinterested.
They can make mistakes, be biased, and serve interests that are not our own.

Now, someone who has lost the ability to judge for themselves can no longer control the decisions made for them; they can only submit to them, unable to discern when the system is wrong or misleading.

The delegation that began as a gain in efficiency leads to a loss of autonomy: we are at the mercy of systems that we no longer understand and can no longer contest, due to not having retained the judgment that would allow us to evaluate them.
There is something even more troubling.
By delegating our decisions, we are also gradually delegating the responsibility that comes with them.
To decide is to take responsibility; to submit to a decision made by a system is to offload that responsibility.
"It's not me, it's the system": this convenient phrase dissolves responsibility into anonymous mechanisms, where no one is accountable for anything.

Now, a society where decisions are made by systems for which no one is responsible is a society where responsibility itself evaporates, where we endure decisions without being able to hold anyone accountable.
The delegation of judgment is also a dilution of responsibility.
Preserving our judgment in the face of increasing delegation does not mean refusing all help, which would be futile and unreasonable.

It means keeping control: understanding, at least in principle, the systems we rely on; maintaining the ability to decide for ourselves, exercising it enough so that it doesn't atrophy; and not delegating the decisions that deeply engage our values and our lives.

For there are choices that we can safely entrust to systems, and others that must remain ours, not because we would decide better, but because deciding is part of what it means to be a free and responsible subject.
To completely give up judging would not only mean losing a skill; it would mean relinquishing a part of what makes us autonomous beings.

sentences: After months of unexplained insomnia, my doctor sent me to spend a night in a sleep lab.
The idea worried me a bit: how could I sleep normally, covered in sensors, in an unfamiliar room, under the watch of a camera?
Upon arriving in the evening, a nurse explained the night's schedule to me, before attaching about twenty small sensors to my body, measuring my brain activity, eye movements, and breathing.
Against all odds, despite this unusual equipment, I eventually fell asleep, probably exhausted from weeks of poor sleep.
The next morning, the specialist doctor analyzed the results with me.
He identified a specific disorder: frequent micro-awakenings, too brief for me to remember, but enough to prevent truly restorative sleep.
This explanation relieved me, in a way.
After months of feeling misunderstood, almost guilty for not being able to 'sleep well', I finally had a concrete explanation for my difficulties.
The doctor proposed a suitable treatment, which gradually improved the quality of my nights.

In the waiting room that morning, I had talked with other patients who described years of similar difficulties before finally deciding to consult, often held back by the idea that their problem wasn't serious enough to justify such a step.
This strange, almost scientific experience allowed me to understand that some sleep problems have specific physiological causes that deserve to be identified rather than just endured in silence.

sentences: So, Mr. Jasper, asked Mrs. Paulina Barnett, are you going to inform our companions about the situation they are in?
Yes, madam.
The time to speak has come, since it is time to act.
And when do you plan to tell them what they don't know?
Right now.
Sergeant Long, added Jasper Hobson, turning to the non-commissioned officer, who immediately took a military stance, gather all your men in the main hall to receive a message.
Sergeant Long automatically turned on his heels and left with a measured step, after touching his hat.
For a few minutes, Mrs. Paulina Barnett and Lieutenant Hobson remained alone, without saying a word.
The sergeant soon returned and informed Jasper Hobson that his orders had been carried out.
Immediately, Jasper Hobson and the traveler entered the main hall.
All the inhabitants of the trading post, men and women, were gathered there, dimly lit by the light of the lamps.

sentences: A warm autumn sun was shining down into the farmyard, over the tall beeches by the ditches.

Beneath the grass trimmed by the cows, the ground, soaked with recent rain, was damp, sinking underfoot with a sound of water; and the apple trees, heavy with fruit, scattered their pale green apples among the dark green of the grass.

Four young heifers were grazing, tied in a line, and mooed occasionally towards the house; the poultry added a splash of color to the manure in front of the stable, scratching, stirring, and clucking, while the two roosters crowed incessantly, searching for worms for their hens, which they called with a sharp cluck.
The wooden gate opened; a man entered, perhaps in his forties, but who looked sixty, wrinkled, stooped, walking with slow, heavy steps weighed down by the load of heavy clogs full of straw.
His long arms hung down on either side of his body.
As he approached the farm, a small yellow dog, tied to the foot of a huge pear tree, next to a barrel that served as his kennel, wagged his tail and then began to bark joyfully.
The man shouted:
--Shut up, Finot!
The dog fell silent.
A peasant woman stepped out of the house.
Her bony, broad, and flat body was outlined under a woolen bodice that tightened at the waist.
A gray skirt, too short, fell to the middle of her legs, which were hidden by blue stockings, and she also wore wooden shoes filled with straw.
A white bonnet, now yellowed, covered some hair plastered to her scalp, and her brown, thin, ugly, toothless face displayed that wild and rough look often seen in peasant faces.
The man asked:
--How's it going?
The woman replied:
--Sir the priest says it's the end, that he won't make it through the night.
They both entered the house.
After crossing the kitchen, they entered the low, dark bedroom, barely lit by a window, in front of which hung a rag of Normandy fabric.
The thick beams of the ceiling, darkened by time, blackened and smoky, spanned the room from one side to the other, supporting the thin floor of the attic, where herds of rats ran day and night.

sentences: The Bétis River flows through a fertile land, under a gentle sky that is always serene.

The land took its name from the river, which empties into the great Ocean, quite near the Pillars of Hercules, and from that place where the furious sea, breaking its banks, once separated the land of Tharsis from great Africa.
This land seems to have preserved the delights of the golden age.
The winters there are mild, and the harsh north winds never blow.
The heat of summer is always tempered by refreshing zephyrs that come to soften the air around midday.
Thus, the entire year is nothing but a happy union of spring and autumn, which seem to hold hands.
The land, in the valleys and in the gentle countryside, yields a double harvest every year.
The roads are lined with laurels, pomegranates, jasmines, and other evergreens that are always in bloom.
The mountains are covered with flocks that provide fine wool sought after by all known nations.

There are several gold and silver mines in this beautiful land; however, the inhabitants, simple and happy in their simplicity, do not even consider gold and silver among their riches; they only value what truly serves the needs of man.
When we began to trade with these people, we found gold and silver among them used for the same purposes as iron; for example, for plowshares.
Since they did not engage in any trade outside, they had no need for any currency.
Almost all of them are shepherds or farmers.

In this country, there are few artisans: for they only tolerate the arts that serve the true necessities of men; moreover, most of the men in this country, being devoted to agriculture or herding, still practice the necessary arts for their simple and frugal lives.

The women spin this beautiful wool and make fine fabrics of wonderful whiteness; they bake bread and prepare meals; and this work is easy for them, as people in this country live on fruits or milk, and rarely on meat.

They use the leather from their sheep to make light shoes for themselves, their husbands, and their children; they make tents, some of which are made of tanned hides and others of tree bark; they make and wash all the family's clothes and keep the houses in an admirable order and cleanliness.

Their clothes are easy to make; for in this mild climate, they wear only a piece of fine, light fabric that is not tailored, and which each person wraps in long folds around their body for modesty, giving it the shape they desire.

sentences: Although the presentation was rather grossly flattering, it is, in general, such a rare thing for a man to come to Paris to spend in a year the fortune of a prince that Mme Danglars cast a glance at the count that was not without a certain interest.
"And you have arrived, sir?..." asked the baroness.
--Since yesterday morning, madam.
--And you come, as usual, from the ends of the earth, as I've been told?
--From Cadiz this time, madam, purely and simply.
--Oh! you arrive in a dreadful season.
Paris is terrible in the summer; there are no more balls, meetings, or parties.
The Italian Opera is in London, the French Opera is everywhere except in Paris; and as for the French Theater, you know it is no longer anywhere.
So we are left with only a few unfortunate outings to the Champ-de-Mars and Satory for entertainment.
Will you be going for a run, sir count?

sentences: The basket was quickly balanced, and Kennedy, followed by Joe, jumped to the ground.
"Your rifles!" shouted the doctor, "your rifles, and be careful!"
Dick rushed for his rifle, and Joe grabbed one of the guns.
They quickly moved towards the trees and entered the cool greenery that signaled abundant springs; they didn't notice the large footprints and fresh tracks that marked the damp ground here and there.
Suddenly, a roar echoed twenty paces away from them.
"The roar of a lion!" said Joe.
"That's good!" replied the exasperated hunter, "we'll fight!"
It's easy to be strong when it comes to fighting.
"Be cautious, Mr. Dick, be cautious! One person's life depends on the lives of all."
But Kennedy wasn't listening; he advanced, his eyes blazing, rifle ready, fearsome in his boldness.
Under a palm tree, a huge lion with a black mane was in an attacking stance.
As soon as he spotted the hunter, he leaped; but before he hit the ground, a bullet struck his heart, and he fell dead.

sentences: Jasper Hobson and Sergeant Long, chatting and observing, stayed on the shore until midnight.
Seeing that everything remained as it was, they then decided to return to Fort Hope to get a few hours of rest themselves.
Both had taken about a hundred steps and were already on the old dried-up bed of the Paulina River when an unexpected noise stopped them.
It was like a distant rumbling that seemed to come from the northern part of the ice field.
The intensity of this noise quickly increased, and soon it reached formidable proportions.
Some powerful phenomenon was obviously occurring in the area, and, in a rather unsettling detail, Lieutenant Hobson thought he felt the ground of the island trembling beneath his feet.
"That noise is coming from the direction of the ice floe!" said Sergeant Long.
"What's happening?..."
Jasper Hobson did not reply, and, extremely worried, he led his companion towards the shore.
"To the fort!"
"To the fort!" exclaimed Lieutenant Hobson.
"Perhaps an ice shift has occurred, and we can launch our boat into the sea!"
And both of them ran breathlessly by the shortest route towards Fort-Espérance.

sentences: The windows downstairs were shining.

One of them was even open; and a strong smell of cooked meat was escaping from it, a smell that suddenly penetrated into the nose and deep into the belly of Walter Schnaffs, causing him to tense up, to gasp, irresistibly drawing him in, throwing a desperate boldness into his heart.
And suddenly, without thinking, he appeared, helmeted, in the window frame.
Eight servants were dining around a large table.
But suddenly a maid stood frozen, dropping her glass, her eyes wide.
All eyes followed hers!
They spotted the enemy!
Lord! The Prussians were attacking the castle!...

At first, there was a scream, a single scream, made up of eight screams uttered in eight different tones, a horrible scream of terror, then a tumultuous uprising, a scramble, a melee, a frantic flight towards the back door.
Chairs were falling, men were knocking over women and stepping on them.
In two seconds, the room was empty, abandoned, with the table covered in food in front of the astonished Walter Schnaffs, still standing in his window.
After a moment of hesitation, he climbed over the supporting wall and moved towards the plates.
His intense hunger made him tremble like a feverish person, but a terror still held him back, paralyzing him.
He listened.
The whole house seemed to tremble; doors were closing, and quick footsteps were running on the floor above.
The anxious Prussian strained to hear these confused noises; then he heard dull sounds as if bodies had fallen into the soft earth at the foot of the walls, human bodies jumping from the first floor.

sentences: Here you go, Your Excellency," said Peppino, taking the chicken from the hands of the young bandit and placing it on a decayed table that, along with a stool and a bed made of goat skins, made up the entire furnishings of the cell.
Danglars asked for a knife and a fork.
"Here you go!
Your Excellency," said Peppino, offering a small knife with a dull point and a wooden fork.
Danglars took the knife in one hand, the fork in the other, and set about cutting the poultry.
"Excuse me, Your Excellency," said Peppino, placing a hand on the banker’s shoulder; "here we pay before eating; we might not be happy when leaving...
"Ah! ah!" said Danglars, "it's not like in Paris anymore, not to mention they will probably skin me alive; but let's do things grandly.
Let's see, I've always heard about the cheap cost of living in Italy; a chicken must be worth twelve sous in Rome.
"Here you go," he said, and he threw a louis to Peppino.
Peppino picked up the louis, and Danglars brought the knife closer to the chicken.
"One moment, Your Excellency," said Peppino, standing up; "one moment, Your Excellency still owes me something.
"When I said they would skin me alive!" murmured Danglars.

sentences: Alas! continued the stranger, undoubtedly to dispel the imperceptible cloud that these words had just cast over Morcerf's brow, we do not do things that way in Italy; we grow according to our race and our species, and we maintain the same foliage, the same size, and often the same uselessness throughout our lives.

--But, sir, replied Count Morcerf, for a man of your merit, Italy is not a homeland, and France may not be ungrateful to everyone; it treats its children poorly, but usually welcomes foreigners greatly.
--Ah! my father, said Albert with a smile, it's clear that you do not know Count Monte-Cristo.
His satisfactions are beyond this world; he does not aspire to honors, and only takes what can fit on a passport.
--That is, in my view, the most accurate expression I have ever heard, replied the stranger.
--Sir has been the master of his future, said Count Morcerf with a sigh, and he has chosen the path of flowers.
--Exactly, sir, replied Monte-Cristo with one of those smiles that a painter will never capture, and that a physiologist will always despair of analyzing.

--If I had not feared to tire the Count, said the general, obviously charmed by Monte-Cristo's manners, I would have taken him to the Chamber; there is an interesting session today for anyone who does not know our modern senators.
--I would be very grateful to you, sir, if you would kindly renew this offer to me another time; but today I have been flattered with the hope of being introduced to the Countess, and I will wait.

sentences: Barbicane felt his heart pounding violently as he set foot on Floridian soil; it seemed he was testing it with his foot, like an architect does with a house to assess its sturdiness.
J.-T. Maston was scratching the ground with the tip of his hook.
"Gentlemen," Barbicane then said, "we have no time to waste, and starting tomorrow we will ride out to explore the area.
At the moment Barbicane landed, the three thousand inhabitants of Tampa-Town had come out to meet him, a well-deserved honor for the president of the Gun Club who had favored them with his choice.
They welcomed him with tremendous cheers; however, Barbicane avoided all ovation, made his way to a room at the Franklin Hotel, and refused to see anyone.
The life of a famous man just didn't suit him.
The next day, October 23, small Spanish horses, full of vigor and spirit, were stamping under his windows.
But instead of four, there were fifty, along with their riders.
Barbicane came down, accompanied by his three companions, and was initially surprised to find himself in the midst of such a cavalcade.
He also noticed that each rider was carrying a rifle slung over his shoulder and pistols in his saddlebags.
The reason for such a display of force was immediately explained to him by a young Floridian, who said to him:
"Sir, there are the Seminoles.
Which Seminoles?
Savages who roam the prairies, and it seemed wise to provide you with an escort.
Pah! said J.-T. Maston as he mounted his horse.
Well, the Floridian replied, it's safer.
Gentlemen, Barbicane replied, I thank you for your attention, and now, let's go!

sentences: So they had talked about the various dangers threatening childhood and the carelessness of the servants.
Madame Homais knew a thing or two about it, still bearing on her chest the marks of a burn from a hot dish that a cook had once dropped on her apron.
Thus, these good parents took a lot of precautions.
The knives were never sharpened, nor were the floors waxed.
There were iron grilles on the windows and strong bars on the door frames.

The little Homais, despite their independence, could not move without a supervisor behind them; at the slightest cold, their father stuffed them with chest protectors, and until they were over four years old, they all wore, mercilessly, padded rolls.
It was, to be fair, a habit of Madame Homais; her husband was inwardly troubled, fearing the possible effects of such compression on the intellect, and he even went so far as to say to her:
— So you intend to make them into Caribs or Botocudos?
Charles, however, had tried several times to interrupt the conversation.
— I need to speak with you, he whispered quietly in the clerk's ear, who then started walking ahead of him up the stairs.
— Would he suspect something? Léon wondered.
He had palpitations and was lost in conjecture.

Finally, Charles, having closed the door, asked him to check for himself in Rouen what the prices of a nice daguerreotype might be; it was a sentimental surprise he was planning for his wife, a thoughtful gesture, her portrait in a black suit.
But he wanted to know beforehand what to expect; these arrangements shouldn't inconvenience Mr. Léon, since he went to the city almost every week.

sentences: He threw his livery cap in front of him, which missed the chair, fell to the ground, and rolled around the room.
"Come on, come on," said Caderousse, "don't get angry, little one!"
"Look, I've thought of you; just take a look at the nice lunch we’re going to have: nothing but things you like, my friend!"

Andrea did indeed smell, as he breathed in, a cooking aroma whose coarse scents had a certain charm for a hungry stomach; it was that mix of fresh fat and garlic that signals lower-quality Provençal cuisine; there was also a taste of gratin fish, and above all, the sharp scent of nutmeg and cloves.
All of this was emanating from two shallow, covered dishes placed on two stoves, and from a pot that was bubbling in the oven of a cast-iron stove.

In the neighboring room, Andrea also saw a fairly clean table adorned with two place settings, two sealed bottles of wine, one green and the other yellow, a good measure of brandy in a carafe, and a fruit salad artfully arranged in a large cabbage leaf on a ceramic plate.
"What do you think, little one?" said Caderousse; "Isn’t it fragrant!"
"Ah! Well! You know, I was a good cook back there! Do you remember how we licked our fingers after my cooking?"
"And you, the first of all, you tasted my sauces, and I believe you didn’t despise them."
And Caderousse began to peel an extra portion of onions.

sentences: After a moment, she said, "I have nothing to know, sir."
But I had found it; I exclaimed, "Miss, I have loved you for a year!"
She was truly surprised and looked up.
I continued, "Yes, miss, listen to me.
I don't know Morin and I don't care about him.
I couldn't care less if he goes to prison and to court.
I saw you here last year, you were over there, in front of the gate.
I felt a jolt when I saw you and your image has never left me.
Believe me or don't believe me, I couldn't care less.
I found you adorable; your memory possessed me; I wanted to see you again; I seized the pretext of that fool Morin; and here I am.
Circumstances have pushed me beyond my limits; forgive me, I beg you, forgive me."
She was watching for the truth in my eyes, ready to smile again; and she murmured, "Tease."
I raised my hand and, in a sincere tone (I even believe I was sincere): 'I swear to you that I'm not lying.'
She simply said: 'Come on.'
We were alone, completely alone, Rivet and my uncle having disappeared into the winding paths; and I made her a true declaration, long and sweet, pressing and kissing her fingers.
She listened to this as something pleasant and new, not quite knowing what to believe about it.
I ended up feeling troubled; thinking about what I was saying; I was pale, oppressed, trembling; and gently, I took her waist.
I spoke softly to her in the little curly hair by her ear.
She seemed lifeless, so lost in thought she was.

Then her hand met mine and squeezed it; I slowly embraced her waist with a trembling and ever-growing hug; she didn't move at all; I brushed my mouth against her cheek; and suddenly my lips, without searching, found hers.
It was a long, long kiss; and it would have lasted even longer if I hadn't heard 'hum, hum' a few steps behind me.
She fled through a thicket.
I turned around and saw Rivet approaching me.
He stood in the middle of the path; and without laughing: 'Well! is this how you handle the business with that pig Morin?'

sentences: Well then, said Andrea, you see, the situation would be for the best, assuming that my request is not rejected by Madame Baroness Danglars and by Miss Eugénie.
We are now in charge of one hundred seventy-five thousand livres in income.

Let's suppose one thing, that I get the marquis to give me the capital instead of paying me the income (it wouldn't be easy, I know that well, but still it is possible), you would help us make the most of these two or three million, and two or three million in capable hands can always yield ten percent.
I never take less than four, said the banker, and even at three and a half.
But for my son-in-law, I would take five, and we would share the profits.

Well, splendid, father-in-law, said Cavalcanti, allowing himself to be carried away by the somewhat vulgar nature that, from time to time, despite his efforts, broke through the veneer of aristocracy he was trying to cover them with.
But immediately recovering himself:
Oh! pardon me, sir, he said, you see, just the hope alone is driving me almost mad, what would the reality be then?

But, said Danglars, who, for his part, did not notice how this conversation, initially disinterested, was quickly turning into a business deal, there is undoubtedly a portion of your fortune that your father cannot refuse you?
Which one? asked the young man.
The one that comes from your mother.
Oh! certainly, the one that comes from my mother, Leonora Corsinari.
And how much can this portion of fortune amount to?
Indeed, said Andrea, I assure you, sir, that I have never focused my mind on this subject, but I estimate it to be at least two million.

Danglars felt that kind of joyful suffocation that either the miser experiences when he finds a lost treasure, or the man about to drown who finds solid ground beneath his feet instead of the void into which he was about to sink.
Well, sir, said Andrea, bowing to the banker with tender respect, may I hope....
Mr. Andrea, said Danglars, hope, and rest assured that if no obstacle on your part hinders the progress of this matter, it is settled.
But, said Danglars, thinking, how is it that Mr. Count of Monte-Cristo, your patron in this Parisian world, did not come with you to make this request?

sentences: Oh! said Danglars, you see that without sharing, in general terms, your sympathy for honesty, I submit to it when I believe the circumstances invite me to do so.
I will continue then.
I proposed a husband to you, not for you, because in truth I wasn't thinking of you at all at that moment.
You love honesty, there you go, I hope; but because I needed you to take this husband as soon as possible for certain business arrangements that I am currently establishing.
Eugénie made a movement.

"It's as I have the honor to tell you, my daughter, and you mustn't hold it against me, because it's you who forces me into this; it's against my will, as you well understand, that I enter into these arithmetic explanations with an artist like you, who fears to enter a banker’s office to perceive unpleasant or anti-poetic impressions or sensations.

"But in this banker’s office, which you kindly entered the day before yesterday to ask me for the thousand francs that I grant you each month for your whims, know, my dear young lady, that one learns a lot about the very use of young people who do not want to marry.

One learns, for example, and out of respect for your nervous sensitivity I will tell you this in this parlor, one learns that a banker's credit is his physical and moral life, that credit supports a man just as breath animates the body, and Mr. de Monte-Cristo once gave me a speech on this that I have never forgotten.
One learns that as credit withdraws, the body becomes a corpse and that this will happen very soon to the banker who prides himself on being the father of such a good logician."
But Eugénie, instead of bending, straightened up under the blow.
"Ruined!" she said.

--You have found the right expression, my daughter, the correct expression, said Danglars, digging into his chest with his nails, while maintaining on his rough face the smile of a man without a heart, but not without wit, ruined! that's it.
Ah! said Eugénie.
Yes, ruined!
Well then, this secret is now known, this horrifying secret, as the tragic poet says.

sentences: Last year, my friends canceled our group vacation at the last minute.
I had already taken my leave and booked my tickets to Portugal.
Two options: stay home sulking, or go anyway.
Alone.
At thirty-one, I had never traveled alone in my life.
I took the plane with a knot in my stomach.
I might as well admit it right away: the first forty-eight hours were tough.
On the first evening in Lisbon, I went into a restaurant and said the phrase that scared me the most: 'A table for one, please.'
I was convinced that everyone was looking at me with pity.
I ate quickly, my eyes on my phone, and I went home early.
But by the second day, something started to change.
I got up when I wanted.
I spent a whole two hours in an azulejos museum that would have bored all my friends.
I changed my plans three times in the same day, on a whim, without negotiating with anyone.
I had never experienced this total freedom.
In a group, every decision is a compromise; alone, every desire is a plan.
And then there were the encounters.
It's the great paradox of solo travel: you're almost never alone.
When you travel in a group, you stay in your bubble.
Alone, you become approachable — and you dare to approach.
An old lady told me the story of her neighborhood on a bench in Porto.
German hikers adopted me for a day of walking.
One evening, in a hostel, we found ourselves six people from five different nationalities cooking together.
I also learned things about myself.
Without anyone to decide for me, I discovered what I really liked — not what the group liked.
In the evening, I wrote a few lines in a notebook.
Rereading those pages today makes me smile: you can see, day after day, fear turning into confidence.
On the last evening, in the same type of restaurant as on the first day, I asked for a table for one with a big smile.
I ate slowly, without my phone, while watching the street.
Traveling alone didn't just allow me to visit Portugal.
It introduced me to someone I didn't know well: myself.
I returned different — a little freer, a little more open.
My friends are already asking me where we are going next year.
I haven't told them yet that I'm hesitating to go alone again.

sentences: Six months ago, I decided to take up running.
I had never run regularly before.
On the first day, I only ran for five minutes.
I was completely out of breath!
I told myself, "This is really not for me."
But I decided to keep going anyway.
Every week, I ran a little bit longer.
Five minutes, then ten, then fifteen.
At first, I ran early in the morning so that no one would see me.
I was a little ashamed to run so slowly.
After two months, I finally managed to run for thirty minutes without stopping.
I was very proud of myself!
My wife noticed the change.
"You look different, fitter," she said to me.
Now, I run three times a week, in the park near my home.
I no longer run in secret.
And I even sometimes go running with my neighbor, who started because of me.

sentences: For fifteen years, I had been waiting to see my favorite band in concert.
This year, it finally happened.
I discovered this band when I was seventeen.
Since then, I have listened to their songs hundreds of times.
When I saw the announcement of a concert in my city, I bought my ticket in ten minutes, before they were all sold out.
On the day of the concert, I arrived three hours before the doors opened, to be close to the stage.
The line was already very long.
I talked with other fans, just as excited as I was.
When the doors finally opened, everyone rushed to the stage.
The concert started at eight o'clock.
From the first notes, I got chills.
For two hours, I sang every word, with thousands of other people around me.
At the end, the singer said, "Thank you for waiting so long with us."
I had tears in my eyes.
This concert will remain one of the most beautiful moments of my life.

sentences: We were two friends followed by eight spahis and four camels with their camel drivers.
We no longer spoke, overwhelmed by heat, fatigue, and parched with thirst like this blazing desert.
Suddenly one of these men let out a sort of cry; everyone stopped; and we remained motionless, surprised by an inexplicable phenomenon known to travelers in these lost lands.

Somewhere near us, in an indeterminate direction, a drum was beating, the mysterious drum of the dunes; it beat distinctly, sometimes more vibrantly, sometimes weakened, stopping, then resuming its fantastic roll.
The Arabs, terrified, looked at each other; and one said, in his language: 'Death is upon us.'
And then suddenly my companion, my friend, almost my brother, fell from his horse, headfirst, struck down by sunstroke.

And for two hours, while I tried in vain to save him, that elusive drum filled my ears with its monotonous, intermittent, and incomprehensible sound; and I felt fear, real fear, hideous fear, creeping into my bones, in front of that beloved corpse, in this hole scorched by the sun between four mounds of sand, while the unknown echo cast upon us, two hundred leagues from any French village, the rapid beating of the drum.
That day, I understood what it meant to be afraid; I realized it even better another time...
The commander interrupted the storyteller:
--Excuse me, sir, but what was that drum?
What was it?
The traveler replied:
I don't know anything.
No one knows.

The officers, often surprised by this strange noise, generally attribute it to an exaggerated echo, amplified and immensely swollen by the undulations of the dunes, of a hail of grains of sand carried by the wind and striking a tuft of dry grass; for it has always been noticed that the phenomenon occurs near small plants burned by the sun, and as hard as parchment.
So this drum would just be a kind of mirage of sound.
That's all.
But I only learned this later.
I come to my second emotion.
It was last winter, in a forest in the northeast of France.
Night fell two hours earlier, so dark was the sky.
I had a peasant as my guide who walked beside me, along a very narrow path, under an arch of fir trees from which the unleashed wind howled.
Between the treetops, I saw clouds fleeing in disarray, frantic clouds that seemed to be escaping from a terror.
Sometimes, under a tremendous gust, the entire forest would bend in the same direction with a moan of suffering; and the cold overwhelmed me, despite my quick pace and heavy clothing.
